For the lines are drawn to describe the fourth part <note>original: "quartam," referring to the quarter-circle shape of the quadrant instrument.</note> of the circle. Here are described the **6 Northern signs** <note>The "septentrionalia" are the signs of the zodiac located north of the celestial equator.</note> which are ascending from **Aries** until the end of **Virgo** on the right side; and in the same part, from the right towards the left, they describe another fourth through the descending signs. Thus, in a certain way, the **zodiac** is divided into four parts. The **6 Southern signs** <note>original: "meridionalia"</note> begin from the same part at **Cancer** <note>While Cancer is technically northern, the author here is likely describing the "descending" arc of the sun's path toward winter.</note> descending toward the winter aspiration, in which there are three signs, namely **Sagittarius**, hanging from the left toward the right, and another three ascending: **Capricorn**, **Aquarius**, and **Pisces**. To the right and left, these are colored upon the face of the instrument so that it may be made as others are colored: some are red and others are black. Some [lines] are written from the left toward the right, others in the contrary direction, and some from back to front. Those which are placed properly from the left toward the right are continuous. In this description, **Aries** is placed toward the front and always corresponds to **Capricorn** <note>In certain medieval instrument layouts, signs are paired based on their distance from the equinoxes or solstices.</note> or **Pisces**. From this point are described the signs moving forward; **Taurus** corresponds to **Leo** or **Virgo**. From above, these are from the right toward the left, including the bodies of **Libra**, **Scorpio**, or **Sagittarius**, etc. The figures are firmly drawn and shall be **red** in color, just as with the Aries of the hours; for this reason, there is a certain middle line which is the equal horizon, and truly that which corresponds to the middle—

## **Chapter Second: To find the degree of the sun by the day of the month, and also to know the conjunction and opposition of the month as it begins, and to find Easter.**

When you have the day and you wish to know in which degree of any sign the sun is on that day, place the thread <unclear>which is</unclear> on the back over that day and see over which of the degrees of the signs the thread falls, because that indicates the location of the sun on that day. It will prepare us to know where the sun's **mansion** <note>Solar and lunar mansions are divisions of the sky the sun and moon pass through; while solar mansions are less common, lunar mansions are a staple of medieval astrology.</note> is; and if you have the degree of which you wish to know when the sun is in it, then place the thread over that degree and see over which day it falls, and you will have the day on which the sun is in that degree. And if you wish to know the mansion from here, on every day see the mansion <unclear>m'</unclear> <unclear>which</unclear> the sun is in a degree with the moon; and where it is in a, there are as many days until it comes to the mansion, and so twice or thrice

it names the mansion and denotes the **lunar mansion** on that day. However, it must be known <unclear>that</unclear> this day is in <unclear>which</unclear> <unclear>p p'</unclear> <unclear>is</unclear> common <note>original: "co'," likely referring to a common year rather than a leap year.</note> because the moon does not move just like the sun's chariot <note>The "sun's chariot" is a poetic reference to the sun's steady orbital course.</note>, and in one day it cannot be in one mansion precisely. If you wish to know the calculation of any month, take on the back the twelve years (as collected) by **28 and 19** <note>These are the Solar Cycle (28 years) and the Metonic Cycle (19 years), the fundamental periods used to calculate the date of Easter in the medieval calendar.</note> and <unclear>m' m' m'</unclear> by hand through the cycle, and see the minute of the year which you took, and note the <unclear>mā</unclear> which differs for you from the calculation of expanded years up to 28, and <unclear>which</unclear> <unclear>is two</unclear> in <unclear>r' m' b'</unclear> it will be the degree of that year for which you will find it, that year with <unclear>io n'</unclear> <unclear>which is in p' t'</unclear> in whatever month they were. <unclear>m' p' l' q' p' 11</unclear> take away 11 and the remainder denotes to you the fraction of the month <unclear>is</unclear> <unclear>mapt'</unclear>. ## **Chapter Third: To know the altitude of the head of Aries in any region, and the other altitude of the sun among the stars placed there, and to find the latitude of places by the altitude of the sun or a star, and to find the degree of the sun by making the horizon and for making the hour of the day.**

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for using the quadrant, transitioning from finding the sun's position in the zodiac to determining its meridian altitude (the highest point it reaches at noon) and the altitudes of fixed stars. It explains how these measurements relate to the local latitude.</meta>

When you wish to know the **meridian altitude** <note>The highest angle the sun reaches above the horizon at noon.</note> of the sun while the sun is at the **beginning of Aries or Libra** <note>original: "principio arietis vel libre"; these are the vernal and autumnal equinoxes.</note>, see where the **horizon** <note>original: "orizon"</note> intersects the line of altitude. Then, by applying that horizon closely, the line will show the latitude of the region <unclear>through</unclear> which it passes, and also the **altitude of the pole** <note>The angle of the North Star/celestial pole above the horizon, which equals the observer's latitude.</note> where no horizon is present. Find the degree on that same line where 
<margin>LL</margin> Aries is understood to descend to the side of the degrees, which are raised for us on the **equinoctial** <term>equinoctial: The celestial equator, the Great Circle in the sky directly above the Earth's equator.</term>. Always using that horizon, this is called the **altitude of the head of Aries** <note>original: "altitudo capitis arietis"; this is the altitude of the celestial equator at noon.</note>, which is the meridian altitude of the sun when the sun is at the beginning of Aries and Libra.

If, however, you wish to find the meridian altitude of the sun when it is in another location, place the **thread** <note>A weighted string or "plumb-line" attached to the center of the quadrant.</note> over that degree on the face of the "mother" <note>The main body or plate of the instrument.</note> and set the **alidade** <term>alidade: A sighting rule or pointer used for measuring angles.</term> over the **ecliptic** <note>The path the sun appears to follow through the stars.</note> for noon. Move the other thread in the middle until the alidade falls upon the degree in the line of altitude, and you will know <unclear>by the latitude</unclear> of Aries toward the south. The degrees which the alidade passes over will give the altitude. 

If you wish to know the **declination** <note>The angular distance of the sun north or south of the celestial equator.</note> of the sun from the equator on that day, likewise move the alidade down from the degrees where Aries was seen to take its altitude; the distance added above the altitude of Aries will give you the meridian altitude of the sun at midday when it is in the 12th degree of Aries. If, however, the altitude shows a descent from the depths, it will take from Aries toward the south; subtract this, because once that distance is added, it changes the altitude from the earth.

<column-break/>

By the head of Aries, you will have the meridian altitude of the sun. If you wish to find the altitude without the display of any of the larger stars placed here, set the alidade upon the **nadir** <note>The point directly opposite the star on the celestial sphere.</note> of that star you have chosen. Then move the thread until the **almuri** <term>almuri: A small pointer or "index" on the instrument used to mark specific values on a scale.</term> falls upon the line of altitude. If the **almuri** moves into the southern part, then for the degrees it passes through, add them to the altitude of the head of Aries. If, however, it falls in the southern part <unclear>of the scale</unclear>, subtract the degrees it passed through from the altitude of the head of Aries, and you will have the greatest height [meridian transit] of that star in that horizon. 

If you have added everything together and the result is 90 degrees, that will be the altitude where the star is at its meridian. If the result is exactly the number of degrees the star is from the equator, then the star at noon passes directly over the center [the zenith]. If the result is greater than the degrees the star is from the equator (because the pole is elevated there), then subtract the result from 180; what remains will be the altitude of the star at its highest point in the **north** <note>original: "septentrio"</note>. If the result was greater than double the altitude of the head of Aries, it means the star is further from the equator than the altitude of the "head" [the equator], and such a star will **never set** <note>original: "nunq' occultabit'"; these are circumpolar stars that circle the pole without dipping below the horizon.</note> in that horizon, and you will have its appearance in altitude in the southern morning.

<keywords>meridian altitude, Aries, Libra, equinoctial, ecliptic, alidade, almuri, declination, circumpolar stars, latitude</keywords>

Regarding stars that are beyond the **southern declination**, it is not the same, because their meridians cannot be captured in this way. To find the **latitudes of places**, which you can easily determine by the instrument: first, take the altitude of the sun at noon. Then, place the thread on the face of the instrument over the degree of the **sign** <note>The zodiac sign</note> in which the sun is located on that day. <unclear>Next</unclear> regarding the eclipse and the thread again at this degree... as it takes the **head of Aries** <note>original: "capit ariet"; this point marks the celestial equator</note>, it will show the **declination** <term>declination: The angular distance of a heavenly body north or south of the celestial equator.</term> of the sun from the equinoctial meridian.

Therefore, if you have this declination in northern signs <note>Aries through Virgo</note>, subtract it from the **meridian altitude**. Or, if you are in southern signs <note>Libra through Pisces</note>, add it to the altitude. By doing this, you will have the **altitude of the head of Aries** <note>The height of the celestial equator at your location</note>. If you subtract this value from 90, the remainder is the **elevation of the pole** above the horizon, which is the **latitude** of that place.

<column-break/>

If you wish to know the same thing by the **stars** marked on this instrument, whose maximum altitude is known: take the altitude of whichever star you wish with your instrument when it is at the meridian <note>When the star is at its highest point in the sky</note>. Then, look up the distance of that star's **declination** from the equinoctial. If the star is of a **northern declination**, subtract that distance from its meridian altitude; otherwise <note>if it is southern</note>, add it. The value you obtain through this addition or subtraction will be the **equinoctial altitude**. Subtract this from 90, and the remainder will be the altitude of the pole, or its elevation above the horizon, which is the latitude of that place.

If you wish to know the same by stars for which we have **two altitudes** <note>These are "circumpolar" stars that never set and can be measured at both their highest and lowest points</note>, namely one which is the lowest altitude and another which is the superior or maximum altitude: take both measurements with your instrument. Then, find the difference between them and take **half of that distance** <note>original: "medietatem ei[us]"</note>. Subtract this half from the greater altitude, or add it to the lesser altitude. The result of this calculation reveals the **elevation of the pole** <note>latitude</note> above that horizon.

If, however, you wish to find the sun's position by the elevation of the pole above the horizon, look through the paths... universally... take the altitude of the sun at noon with your instrument. Then see what the altitude of the **head of Aries** is at that horizon by subtracting the elevation of the pole from 90. If the sun is above the equinox... see its maximum meridian altitude... and by this you shall receive the degrees.

Above this, by reason of the arcs of the signs or the **tropics** <term>the circles of latitude marking the sun's northernmost and southernmost points</term>, you must draw the primary lines, both small and large, in the spaces beyond. Once this is done, you will have the proper middle spaces for the signs, namely:

**Capricorn** in the first part;
**Sagittarius** in the second part;
**Taurus** <note>OCR "Lanau" likely refers to Taurus or Libra in this sequence</note> in the third part;
**Gemini** <note>OCR "Lanau" and "Gemīi" are transcribed here</note> in the fourth.

You yourself can establish the cause and order in the inscriptions of the signs until you have all the spaces of all the signs. When you wish to scribe the points of the degrees of the other signs, do as was previously done for Capricorn through the middle of the tool prepared for this end, following the first line until you find the desired point.

<column-break/>

At the 30th degree and 4th minute, continue in this manner until all things are marked in their proper places. Proceed thus with the other signs, but work from the beginning of the duration. When you have the degrees and the markings according to the method of the hours, which are in the middle of the **azimuths** <term>original: *azorciz*; arcs used to measure horizontal positions</term> of the signs, it remains to place them in the half-arcs. Draw them twice in the upper arcs, and in others draw two with the halves.

The **limb** <term>original: *limbū*; the outer graduated rim of the astrolabe</term> must be located there, and the scribe should connect your thread <note>likely a reference to a plumb line or alignment cord</note>. You will prepare this from the arc. The signs are to be marked at the beginning by taking the peaks. Note that **Cancer** is marked in **red** <term>original: *rubro*; red ink was often used to highlight specific signs or solar positions</term> with its parts, while **Gemini** follows.

The arc moves from the **left toward the right**, and then from the **right toward the left**. In the second arc, mark the line with a **black hand** <term>original: *nigro māu*; black ink</term>, beginning freely from the degrees from 1 to 10. There are two for the first, and another arc above 29 for the first at the top of the body. Inscribe it slightly in **red** for **Cancer**, moving from the right toward the left.

Then there are **Leo** and **Virgo**, half from the left toward the right. Note that Gemini is measured similarly. These are the signs. For when you must write the degrees of the **zodiac** <term>original: *zodiaci*</term>, use the first method with a **red hand**, but from the right toward the left. You will begin first in **Sagittarius**, and then from 1 to 10 in the third part. The reason for this extension is clear. Then, from the left toward the right with **black**, mark the degrees toward 180; then from the first toward the left to degree 210 with **red**. Then from the left toward the right with **black** for the third part.

### On the Placement of Fixed Stars

Then move the lid, which is by itself [movable], only in the manner [of the others], with more [marks] upon the part of the style's head, so that it does not [sit] on the surface like another, either obliquely or as it should be. And now from the graduation of the cylinder, let it be <unclear>broken off</unclear>.

<column-break/>

### Following is the use of the cylinder
->[At the] time of the sun's altitude<-

In this way, using the cylinder, turn the lid with the **style** <term>style: the horizontal shadow-casting pin</term> until the style is above the line of degrees <unclear>pointing toward</unclear> the sun, so that its shadow will show the degree of altitude at the present time. Because these are the **shadow points** <term>shadow points: divisions of the gnomon's length into 12 parts, used to calculate height or distance</term>, turn the part toward the line of points, then opposite to the <unclear>pole</unclear> and the shadow of the sun. With the shadow point, <unclear>perform</unclear> the task, one of 122 <unclear>and have</unclear> the shadow points <unclear>in this way</unclear> from the hour for the project which is said and <unclear>done</unclear> until it rests on the plane. And always <unclear>set</unclear> the shadow points <unclear>there</unclear> and see what the space of the bodies is to <unclear>the end</unclear>. Because if the points fall <unclear>equally</unclear> with the length of the shadow as said before, the proportion will be fewer <unclear>in number</unclear>, let it be done so. The shadow points are referred back to 12; thus the rest of the matter holds itself to its shadow. And if you wish [to find] the hour of the day, place the style over the **month** <note>Pillar dials require the user to align the gnomon with the current month/zodiac sign because the sun's midday height changes throughout the year.</note> with the designated points and over the part of the month above which the proportion of the points is said. And opposite the sun, then through the shadow over the **hour lines** <term>hour lines: the curved lines on the cylinder that indicate the time based on the shadow's length</term>, <unclear>it shows</unclear> the hour of the day upon the lines. And your hour, if it was before midday, it might be 11, or <unclear>mark</unclear> if it is after midday. If however the shadow falls upon those lines, then it is <unclear>marked</unclear>; lead the hour [to find] if it is before midday, such as 10, or if it is after midday.

## On making meridian sundials
## which are called sundials
## facing the 4 parts of the world.
## And first regarding the
## declining equinoctial
## sundial, which is a
## sundial facing the North <note>original: "Arctum," referring to the constellation of the Bear, signifying the North.</note>.

First, let there be made on the base measurement <note>original: "mūpa," likely *mensura* or *mappa*</note> a quantity of total or partial parts according to the measurement which is divided into these 12 equal parts. And let perpendicular lines be drawn toward the height at the points of division of the half-circle. And in the middle of the figure, place the gnomon <note>original: "pili," literally 'hairs' or 'pins,' referring to the style that casts the shadow.</note> at the center of the circle according to equal right angles. And let the length of the gnomon be as one pleases, provided that it is half the diameter of the circle. And in that time, the gnomon is said to be... <unclear>elogi'</unclear> through the center... but in two sides of the line it is necessary because there they are contained according to the diameter of the circle.

<column-break/>

## On making sundials on a flat
## plane according to the second method.

Let a circle be made as held before <note>referring to the previous geometric construction</note> which is divided into 4 equal parts, of which the two lower ones are each divided into 6 parts; which parts ought to be noted subtly on the half-circle in this manner: by drawing lines from the center of the circle to the points marked on the circumference. In a more precise way, let one line be joined with our contrary line on the part of the circle drawn... <unclear>s’m ū d’</unclear>... reaching the various points... of the position of the ruler from the center point through those markings to the tangent line <note>original: "lincā cōtīgenciē"</note>. Where the ruler intersects the joining line, there make your marks... then divide each one into 90 degrees... From which indeed from the point where they join, one to as many degrees as are contained in any... to which you wish such a sundial to face. Such a declination <term>declination: the angle at which a sundial's face deviates from facing exactly South</term> is commonly... for the day 34 degrees of the great world.

## Another sundial to be made facing east and west

This specific [method] for a sundial facing east: first, let one line be noted according to the inclination, and in such a way that the first part of the line faces toward the south <note>original: "meridiem"</note>; let it be drawn out beyond our usual [limit] <insert>and</insert>. Then let a circle be made, not very large, in the lower part of the line, the center point of which is placed on the line; and draw a "hidden line" <gloss>original: linea occulta; a faint construction line used for drafting</gloss> toward the side as before. Then, divide one quarter <note>a quadrant of the circle</note> into six parts. Then, draw lines from the center point through those markings to meet the line, and where it intersects, fix the line where a mark is made. And if there were points found on either line, they should similarly be made on the middle line; then it shall be drawn through those markings.

### On the method of making a sighting instrument according to the orthogonal projection of a square, which must be constructed as follows according to the rules for its formation

**F**irst, provide some wood or thick paper and cut it into a square shape, much like small cards or a square block. Having done this, consider the elevation of the pole <note>original: "elevatōz poli"; this refers to the latitude of the observer's location</note> as determined by the longitudes and latitudes of the regions found in your books. On your paper or wooden square, place one foot of a compass at one corner as a fixed point and move the other foot to the other side to describe a quadrant <note>a quarter-circle</note> by swinging it. Once this is done, divide that quarter-circle into six equal parts, and each of those markings will represent 15 degrees <note>6 parts × 15 degrees = 90 degrees</note>. Thus, following the first three markings toward the left hand, you will have 0, 15, 30, 45, 60, and so on up to 90 for the elevation of the pole. Then, at the marking [corresponding to your latitude], take a ruler <term>lincale: a straightedge or sighting rule</term> which you shall place at the corner of the square, and through the point of division you have marked, draw a line from the corner of the square to that first point of the division.

<column-break/>

By measuring the divisions, you will have the elevation of the pole; this is illustrated in the figure where the pole is elevated 40 degrees. The figure is applied to others as previously shown, with a line drawn from the center in the figure. The line of the edge of the square follows through the other arcs of the square and returns to that part... Then, having done this, take the corner of the square [marked] by the line of the elevation of the pole already established. Once this is done, consider the remaining portion: the division to the left designates the elevation of the pole, while the second portion to the right is the elevation of the equinoctial <note>original: "elevatō equinoctialis"; the celestial equator, which is always at an angle of 90 degrees minus the latitude</note>. For the calculation of the angles of the sighting instrument <note>original: "visiatorij"</note>, take the points for the left hand and the right hand, decreasing them... the angles from which they are joined on your wood or paper. These are established in the figure below you... the arcs of the long lines... which rotate sharply... and the angle in the first place... will be directly opposite to it in a straight line, namely the angle of the pole.

### **The Sundial**

That **sundial** <term>horalogium: a general term for any device that tells time, usually a sundial in this context</term> is made in this way: make a circle within the square of the revolving [sphere] and draw through the middle two diametric lines following the vessel <note>original: "vasiat"; likely referring to the container or frame</note> in the middle, which divides it into two halves. This is said because one part is divided by ten, and he says one part of these is divided by equal means. Turn yourself to one [point] and take your **compass** <note>original: "compassum"</note> and place the foot in the center of the earth <note>In medieval cosmology, the center of the instrument often represented the center of the Earth or the observer's position</note> and with the other part make a point upon the diameter. From these points, draw lines to the points marked in the division. You shall take from the fourth part of the **North** <note>original: "septen-trio-nem"</note> descending until the ninth; it is made here. There are two others yet: one for the use of the middle, the other for the use of the lines. The first agrees with the... when it prepares for the two, and so by using it, it is to be seen, shown, and arranged.

**It is necessary** from here to take from theory, and rather theory, and what more is commanded through... and what proceeds you shall accept by sight. As was said before, the unknown quantity of any thing may be known by a polished instrument. For the foundations of measurement <note>original: "ara"; likely a shorthand for "area" or "ars"</note> are said to be divided into three parts, just as in the second [book] of **Altimetry** <term>altimetria: the science of measuring heights and distances</term> and **Planimetry** <term>planimetria: the science of measuring plane surfaces</term>.

**Altimetry** is when only the height of a distant thing is sought. And **Distance-measurement** <note>original: "irometr"; likely a corruption of "chorometria" or "geometria"</note> is when only the length, breadth, and depth of a thing is sought. **Planimetry** is when the length of a flat thing is sought.

The first measurement is **linear dimension**.
The second is **superficial dimension**.
The third is **corporeal dimension**.

We treat, therefore, the manner of knowing the measures of things in their form. You know that pertaining to the measures of that area, it is divided into two parts. For in the first part, it will treat the **quadrant** <term>quadrans: an instrument used for taking altitudes and telling time, shaped like a quarter-circle</term> which is said to be formed from the fourth part of a circle. In the second part, we shall speak of what is proper to the circle and of many other things.

The **quadrant**, therefore, is an instrument containing the fourth part of a circle, with certain lines drawn through it, by which we are able to [measure] the Sun and the stars concerning their altitude. Through those altitudes, we can know the hours, the times, the distances of things, heights, breadths, and the lengths of lands through many [means].

# For obtaining the altitude of the sun
Everything regarding the composition of the quadrant must be said concerning its utility and the spaces that are <unclear>written</unclear> before. If you wish to know the altitude <note>original: "altitudo," the vertical angle of a celestial body above the horizon</note> of the sun on any given day, place point "a" of the quadrant toward the sun and point "o" toward the earth. Capture the ray of the sun, and once you have the ray, see which <term>gradus</term> <note>gradus: a degree, one of the 360 units of a circle</note> the plumb line <note>original: "perpendiculum," a weighted string used to indicate a vertical line</note> touches. You may know the degree in which the sun is located in the <unclear>whole table</unclear> by the course of the sun in its proper month and from the midday of that same month. Place the plumb line over that day, and it will be noted according to the rule under that month; the degree of the sign where the string falls is the degree in which the sun resides.

# To obtain the sun's declination and its distance from the equinoctial line
If you wish to know the declination <term>declinatio: the angular distance of a heavenly body north or south of the celestial equator</term> of the sun—that is, how far it is distant from the equinoctial <note>original: "equinoctiali," the celestial equator</note> line—place the string over the degree in which the sun is on that day according to the aforementioned <term>materiam</term> <note>the "matter" or instruction previously given</note>. Note the degree on the <term>limbus</term> <note>limbus: the outer edge or rim of the instrument where the scale is marked</note> upon which the string falls. Afterward, place the string over the middle line, and it will show us which degree on the rim the plumb line crosses. The number of degrees on the rim between the first note and the second will be the sun's declination for that day, which is used for finding the latitude of another region.

# If you wish to know the latitude of a region and the distance of the poles from the equinoctial above

<column-break/>

the altitude of the pole—which is the same thing—take the altitude of the sun at midday while the sun is at the beginning of **Aries** or **Libra** <note>These are the points of the spring and autumn equinoxes</note>. Subtract that altitude from 90, and the remainder is the latitude of the region, or the altitude of the pole. Alternatively, take the altitude of the sun at midday and subtract from it the sun's declination for that day if the sun is in a <unclear>northern</unclear> sign, or add it if it is in a <unclear>southern</unclear> sign. Subtract the result from 90, and you will have the latitude of the region or the altitude of the pole. Or, in this way: take the altitude of some fixed star near the pole at its highest point <note>original: "maiori altitudine," its upper culmination</note> during the night, and the altitude of the same star at its lowest point <note>original: "minori altitudine," its lower culmination</note> in the same night. Subtract the lower altitude from the higher, and the result is the altitude of the pole according to the region's latitude.

Once the total degrees are known on the rim of the quadrant where you take the altitude—where the tables are inscribed—[the text becomes technical regarding the specific markings for the beginning of Aries] ...on the quadrant will be [the hour] for that region. ### To know in which sign all other planets and fixed stars are located
<margin>how to inquire</margin>

**If** you wish to know by the signs the location of all other planets and all fixed stars that do not have their own light <note>original: "radios proprios," perhaps referring to the lack of "rays" or distinct planetary motion compared to the "fixed" background.</note>, once the planet is aligned through the **two sights** <note>The two small holes or "foramina" on the edge of the instrument used for sighting.</note>, wherever the plumb line falls, there is the sign of that planet. And note that the Moon does not always agree with the other planets in its degrees, as it may be off by two or three degrees, except when it is at the **mid-point** <note>original: "fermisse," possibly referring to the syzygy or a specific phase where the Moon's latitude is zero.</note>, for then it agrees in its degrees. Nor is there a better way to arrange the whole sky and to know which sign is in the East and the degree of the **ascendant** <term>ascendant</term> <note>The degree of the zodiac rising over the eastern horizon at a specific moment.</note>.

**If** you wish to arrange the whole sky, proceed again by parts and by the sign that is in the East, and that which is in the West, and that which is in the middle. In this preparation, without the **midnight line** <note>The "linea medie noctis" is the vertical line representing the North-South meridian opposite the noon position.</note>, first place the signs in their succession: Aries, Taurus, Gemini. Then consider any star or planet and in which sign it is; then divide the whole estimated sky into equal parts. Once this is done, look at the sign in the middle; you will see that the third sign from it is in the East, following the order of the signs. And counting backwards, the third sign—Aries, Pisces, Aquarius, and so on—will be in the West. Finally, the sign opposite the one in the middle will be on the **midnight line**.

<column-break/>

### To know when a planet approaches us or recedes from us

**If** you wish to know whether any planet is approaching us or receding from us, observe it on the **meridian line** <term>meridian line</term> <note>The imaginary North-South line that passes directly overhead; a star reaches its highest point when it crosses this line.</note>. Then observe its altitude on that day. If the planet is fast-moving, or over several days if it is slow, observe its altitude when it is on the meridian line. If you find it closer to the **zodiac line** <note>original: "linea zodiaca," the Ecliptic.</note> than it was before, it is approaching. If, however, it has moved further away, it is receding.

### To know whether any planet is Southern or Northern

**If** you wish to know whether any planet, or indeed any visible star, is Southern or Northern, first assume the **equator** <note>original: "equinoctialis," the celestial equator.</note> is positioned above the horizon. Whether the planet is approaching or receding, take a careful measurement of its altitude on the meridian line. Because if that planet is higher than the equator, it is **Northern** <note>original: "septentrionalis."</note>; if it declines lower, then it is **Southern** <note>original: "australis."</note>.

### To know the elevation of all planets or stars

**If** you wish to know the **elevation** <note>original: "elenatonem," a scribal error for "elevationem" or altitude.</note> of all planets and stars over our hemisphere at whatever hour of the day you wish, look at the planet or star whose elevation you wish to know through the two sights. If it is correctly found, the plumb line is trusted in... <unclear>tretibo</unclear>

<meta>This page continues the technical manual for an astronomical instrument, likely a quadrant or a simplified astrolabe. While the previous page focused on identifying the zodiac signs of celestial bodies, this page provides instructions for determining planetary motion (retrograde or stationary), distinguishing planets from fixed stars by their twinkling, and calculating the relationship between degrees of ascension and time.</meta>

If you wish to know at what degree the **almucantar** <term>almucantar</term> <note>original: "almuca," referring to the circles of altitude on an astronomical instrument.</note> will be, when all the quantities are subtracted according to the previously mentioned situation, that will be the elevation or height of that planet or star above it. To know the **equinoctial elevation** <note>The height of the celestial equator above the horizon at a specific location.</note>:

**If** you wish to know the desired visual elevation of the pole using the said instrument which is called the **almucantar-quadrant** <note>original: "almucamidiara," likely a corruption of "almucantarat."</note>, or if you see when the Sun or Moon or any planet is in the highest degree of **Aries** <note>The text likely means the first degree of Aries or Libra, the equinoctial points.</note> or **Libra**, then take its altitude at midday. That altitude is the same as the **equinoctial ray** <note>The angle of the equator.</note> on the meridian line.

->Whether a planet is stationary or retrograde<-

**If** you wish to know whether any planet is **stationary**, **retrograde**, or **direct** <term>planetary motion</term> <note>Direct motion is moving forward through the zodiac; retrograde is appearing to move backward; stationary is the pause between these states.</note>, see in which sign and degree it is located. Then, after the fourth or sixth night—if the planet is slow like **Saturn** or **Jupiter**—or after two nights if it is fast like **Mars**, look again. If the planet is in exactly the same number and degree as it was in the prior space of time, then it is **stationary**. If it has more degrees in the next sign than it had before, then it is **direct**. If it has fewer, then it is **retrograde**.

->To know whether a certain star is a planet or not<-

**If** you wish to know whether any

<column-break/>

of the stars is a planet or not, first look into the **zodiac** <note>The belt of the heavens through which the Sun, Moon, and planets move.</note> to see whether there are any stars there that **twinkle** <note>original: "scillat" or "scintillat."</note> or not. For if it twinkles, then it is not a planet. If indeed it does not, then it is a planet. A **second way** this can be known is through their course over seven hours, as mentioned above; that which is measurable for the Sun must be measured for the other planets.

->To know how many degrees of the Sun’s ascension make one hour<-

**If** you wish to know how many degrees of the Sun's ascension above the world—that is, above the meridian—make one **unequal hour** <term>unequal hour</term> <note>Also called "temporal hours," these divide daylight into 12 equal parts, meaning they are longer in summer and shorter in winter.</note> on any given day, first arrange the aforementioned **bead** <note>original: "marguita," a sliding marker on the plumb line of a quadrant.</note> in the mark to take the hours of that day. Find the angle for the degree of ascension for an **equal hour**. Having done this, place the said bead upon the first part of the hour angle you wish to make, which the elevation of the Sun holds. Mark the spot on the **limbus** <note>The graduated outer edge or rim of the instrument.</note> where the **plumb line** <note>original: "perpendiculum."</note> falls. By this sign, place the bead on the plumb line over the end of the hour and look at the degree it touches on the said rim. Note how many degrees are in between; for that many degrees of elevation the Sun moves in that hour. It follows the same by proportion, and similarly you can judge how many degrees those hours were above.

->To know how many degrees make one equal hour<-

**If** you wish to know how many degrees make one **equal hour** <note>A standard 60-minute hour where each hour corresponds to 15 degrees of the Earth's rotation (360 / 24).</note>, divide 360 and 60 by 24.

The third part of our instrument is the **alidade** <note>original: "alidada"; a revolving pointer used for sighting objects or reading scales.</note>, provided with forty holes, etc. Perforated at point A and derived from the **zodiac** <note>original: "zodiacum"</note> to which it pertains, its median line—or **fiducial line** <note>original: "linea fiducie"; the precise edge or line used for measurement</note>—is marked on both sides with what is called a median lining, spaced with graduations of the medians. Numbers are inscribed upon the alidade, and upon it are two **sighting vanes** <note>original: "pinnule"</note>, which are portable, through which the solar ray may pass at any given time. The author has marked this upon a flat, round plate divided into 360 degrees <note>OCR reads "363 g," likely a transcription error for 360 degrees</note>, which represents the surface of the earth. It is separated diametrically by a mediating line, passing through the earth at two points of the zodiac. Each year, [the measurements] depend on the distance from the surface of the zodiac on the figure of the plate, acting as the **ecliptic** <note>original: "ecliptica"; the sun's apparent path across the sky</note>. Indeed, the numbers descend to the south from the median of the plate, whether by the large stem or the lengths of this alidade, with its sighting vanes, until they reach the figure.

...toward the setting of the sun and the equinox. Primarily from one [mark] to another are the arcs of the day; and those which remain are the arcs of the night. ### Concerning the hours of the day and night already passed at any moment

**P**lace the **almuery** <term>almuery</term><note>original: "almiuri", from the Arabic *al-muri*; the index or pointer found on the edge of an astrolabe's rete</note> upon the mark for sunrise; then rotate the entire disk of figures with the **rete** <note>the rotating star-map plate of an astrolabe</note> until the middle rays of the sun pass through the holes of the **sighting vanes** <note>original: "foramina", referring to the holes in the alidade used to align with the sun</note>. Note the almuery, and this is the method for the current moment. Then, measure the distance the almuery has traveled from the sunrise mark to the current mark through the divisions of the hours. This will give you the **unequal hours** <note>also known as "planetary hours," where the day and night are each divided into 12 hours regardless of season</note> already completed, or the equal ones by the same measure. Do the same for the night, noting the marks accordingly. In the same way, you shall have these measurements upon the **ecliptic** <note>the sun's apparent path across the sky</note>, and you shall have the time of the sun by measuring from midday when it is at its greatest distance... without the G <note>possibly a specific reference mark on the instrument</note>. In the same way, align the **pearls** <note>original: "margaritas"; likely small decorative or functional studs on the instrument used as tactile markers</note> and you will have the natural hours of the day in the quadrant toward the south.

### Concerning the verification of the wandering stars or fixed stars both in longitude and in latitude

**W**hoever wishes to verify the locations of the **wandering stars** <note>planets</note> or **fixed stars** both in longitude and in latitude, assuming the [position] is known, should proceed in this manner: construct the "figure of the heaven" <note>a celestial map or horoscope</note> according to the true position of the sun and the marks of the almuery for that same hour. Then rotate

<column-break/>

the pointer alone without the disk of figures to the location of the moon, observing it through the altitude of the large triangle, calculating or measuring the moon's remainder through the holes of the sighting vanes. This should be done in the triangle of the figure because the distance in longitude of the moon from the sun's position is its true gravity <note>original: "gravitas", perhaps referring to its specific weight or relative position in this context</note> or the altitude of the large rete. From the position of the moon, observe its latitude and how far it is from the ecliptic. For example, if it is at the same distance from the great ecliptic as the indicated location, and its latitude is that of the sun's path, then there is no doubt regarding the density of the moon's position. If it is distant from the ecliptic by three degrees... [lacuna/abbreviated] ...whether it be in the northern or southern part. Do the same if it is in another [region]. Then, following the observed time, construct the figure of the heaven by the moon's position as predicted for that moment. Note the almuery for that same moment... [it is] toward the west at its mark for the current time, which are 14 [units], which should be added or diminished above the moon's location joined to the setting of the sun. If you do this correctly, you will have the location of the moon for the present hour. Truly, by which time you make the figure of the heaven, rotate the pointer without the disk of figures to the aforementioned [marks] which are verified... in the same way as the moon, you will have the location in longitude relative to the sun and then its latitude. In the same year, place the pointer at the fixed stars. In the same way, you shall do this for the other fixed stars and for the planets.

## Here begins the treatise on the magnet and its wondrous powers, subtleties, and principles

### This treatise on the magnet contains two parts, the first of which comprises ten chapters through which [the subject is explored] by its parts and the intention of the work:
The **second** <note>The first chapter is "the intention of the work" mentioned in the heading</note> concerns what kind of craftsman <term>artifex</term><note>meaning a skilled maker or practitioner who combines theory with manual labor</note> the creator of this work should be; the **third** on the recognition of the stone; the **fourth** on the distinction of the parts of the stone; the **fifth** on finding the poles of the stone—first the northern and then the southern; the **sixth** on how a magnet attracts a magnet; the **seventh** on how iron, touched by a magnet, is directed toward the poles of the world; the **eighth** on how a magnet attracts iron; the **ninth** on how the northern part can attract the southern part; the **tenth** on the inquiry into where the magnet receives the natural power that it possesses. 

The **second part** [contains three chapters]: **first**, on the construction of an instrument by which the **azimuth** <term>azimuth</term><note>an astronomical measurement representing the horizontal angle or direction of a celestial body from the observer</note> of the sun, the moon, and any star on the horizon is known; **second**, on the construction of a better instrument for this purpose; **third**, on a wheel of <column-break/> **perpetual motion**.

### Follows concerning the study of this work and its investigation

Dearest of friends, at your request, I shall disclose to you in a brief narrative the hidden power of a certain stone, a greatness of the stone hidden from many. For nothing is known to philosophers without principles... and the nature of good things is obscured until the mind fixes its ray of light upon the principles. I shall explain things that are commonly seen as simple [to the common folk] but are understood through reason... specifically concerning the **magnet stone** <note>original: "magnete lapide"</note> in this short work... the root of the matter... the teaching of natural philosophy... of the causes of this stone... the art of the stone... these works which you see will seem like unspeakable things to the common folk, and like illusions or phantasms. But [this knowledge] is concerning astrology <note>here used in the sense of astronomy or celestial influence</note> and is natural... and provides no small benefit to humanity. Let a man know how to gather the merits of this work.

### On the craftsman of this work

Know, dearest friend, that the craftsman of this work must know the nature of things and not be ignorant of the celestial motions; but he himself must also be industrious in the work of his hands, so that through his own industry he may realize this wonderful effect. For through his industry, he may correct an error which he would not be able to do by natural reason or mathematics alone if he did not take care with his hands.

### On the knowledge of this stone and of its diverse kinds

<margin>Note</margin>
This stone can be recognized by four differences: namely, [by its appearance], weight, and power. Its **color**, moreover, should be iron-gray, bluish, and mixed with the color of wood <note>original: "lignis"; other versions often describe this as a dull or silvery luster, like unpolished metal</note>, so that it does not appear like polished iron that has been corrupted and infected by the air. Such a stone is never seen in other parts, but it is mostly seen in southern regions and is produced <unclear>before</unclear> in the <unclear>neighboring</unclear> parts of the sea; according to the power [known in] **Normandy and Flanders**, that stone should also be [solid] in its weight, since it often has many rusty parts and many pores on the outside, that is, **clay** <note>original: "id est clay"; the scribe uses the vernacular "clay" to explain earthy impurities within the ore</note>. It should be more heavy in proportion to its size, and is to be drawn into a miraculous shape... you will have this stone determined for this treatment... because among all kinds, this stone is that which...

### On the natural disposition of the magnet

<column-break/>

<insert>11.10</insert>
You must know that this stone carries within itself a **likeness of the heavens**, as is evident through experience and suitable proofs. And therefore... there are points... because they are seen above the celestial [sphere]... upon axes, one of which is the **Arctic pole** toward the **North** <note>original: "nord"; Peregrinus uses the vernacular word for the direction</note>, while the other remains in the **Southern land**. Just as you may fully understand in this stone... and of the points <unclear>remaining</unclear> middle to the two points... whatever [kind you have]...

The method is to make it round, just as a **crystal** <note>original: "cristallus"; referring to a spherical orb or lens</note> and other stones are rounded; and afterward, you place a needle or an iron wire in the manner of a needle upon the stone, and according to the length of the iron, draw a line on the stone dividing it through the middle. Then place the needle or iron again upon the stone [in a different position]... and mark a line. And if you wish, you may do this in another place... so that without a doubt both lines [intersect] in two points. These represent the **poles of the world** in opposition. Then, because... when it is proven in the stone, you will see [the result]. Some great [property] of these middle points is seen in the rounded stone. Thus... the tip of the needle or iron... so that it is oblong.

## On the specific knowledge of both poles of the magnet

Having seen the art of knowing the poles of the lodestone—namely, which is North and which is South—you shall recognize them by this method. Make a round wooden vessel in the fashion of a **dish or platter** <note>original: "parapsidis"; a shallow bowl</note>, and in it place the stone in such a way that there is an equal distance from the rim of the vessel to the stone itself. Then place that vessel, with the stone positioned inside, into another large vessel filled with water, so that the stone in the first vessel is like a **sailor in a ship** <note>a famous medieval metaphor for a floating object allowed to rotate freely</note>. The first vessel should be properly made to float like a ship in a river, so that in no part—and I say this specifically—nor through the four directions <note>the cardinal points</note> should proximity to the rim of the large vessel hinder the natural movement of the stone. Hence, the stone thus positioned will turn the first vessel until the **North pole** of the stone looks toward the North, and the **South pole** toward the South, and there it will stay. For even if it were moved a thousand times, it would return a thousand times to its own place by the will of God <note>a phrase indicating that this is a fixed law of nature</note>. Then the Northern and Southern parts are known in the heavens, and through them they are known in the stone, because any such stone can [point them out].

<column-break/>

...indicate to them thus through all things, as appears in the figure below:

## That a magnet attracts a magnet invariably

Having gained knowledge of which pole in the stone is North and which is South, mark the poles first so that you may recognize them whenever necessary. And if you wish to see by experience how the stones act, take two stones and prepare them in the same way. Place one in its vessel so that it floats like a sailor in a ship, and let the points be at an equal distance from the heavens or the rim of the vessel. Then take the other stone in your hand and bring the **Northern** part of the stone you are holding toward the **Southern** part of the stone floating in the vessel. Immediately, the floating stone will adhere to the stone you are holding quite swiftly. And if you bring the **Southern** part of the held stone toward the **Northern** part of the floating stone, it proceeds in the same way. Understand from this that the Northern part in one stone attracts the Southern part in another stone, and the Southern the Northern. If you do the opposite—that is, if you apply the **Southern** part of the stone in your hand [to the Southern part of the floating stone]—you will see the floating stone flee.

### How the stone attracts

<margin>
<image-desc>Two horizontal line drawings, representing iron needles or bars used in magnetic experiments.</image-desc>
</margin>

Because it is known to everyone by experiment that an oblong piece of iron touches and is acted upon by the magnet, and likewise remains fixed by its own attachment, once it is exposed, one part is measured toward that **nautical compass** <term>pixis nautica</term><note>literally "nautical box"; one of the earliest references to a boxed mariner's compass</note> which is near the pole. For the reason it moves is not just toward the compass, but toward the **celestial pole** <term>polus mundi</term>. Indeed, because the parts of the heavens are in their own way moved, the remaining part of the iron moves toward that part of the sky, or is moved toward that other part. Therefore, the part of the iron that has touched the southern part of the stone moves toward the Northern part of the heavens. Behold, if it were from the part of the iron that touched the North of the stone, it would turn toward the South. This is the strength of the movement of the iron, and this abundance of power is not random, but proves itself through these means.

### On the alteration of the iron's power by reason of the stone

If, however, the final appearance of the stone—just like iron floating or swimming upon the water—shows an attraction of the northern part of the iron when the southern part of the stone is applied to it, the cause is in the proximity...

<column-break/>

...or if you extend the same to the southern part of the iron, the other part of the stone causes attraction even without assistance. If, however, you apply the North pole of the stone to the North pole of the iron, the iron will **flee** <note>original: "fuguerei"; referring to magnetic repulsion</note> until the southern part is joined to it. The same is understood concerning the parts of the stone. Therefore, the first power is made to vanish by the second; the northern part of the iron, which had been attracted to the South of the stone, is put to flight by the South of the stone and is instead drawn to the North. Thus, the "meridional" <note>Southern</note> label applied to the stone's power may be changed in the iron, and that which was North becomes South. This change is the **impression** <term>impressio</term><note>the medieval idea that a magnet "imprints" its likeness or "virtue" onto the iron</note> of the last agent, which overcomes and alters the previous power.

### On the proof of this art

The proof that the South of the stone attracts is that, as has been said, the attraction of the magnet is stronger; but the flight or repulsion is weaker when the iron is handled according to the previously mentioned way. The agent <note>the magnet</note> intends its own action not only to assist the object, but so that from the agent and the object a single thing is made. This is shown by the following experiment with the stone: Take a stone and mark it as a whole from *a* to *d*, in which *a* is the North and *d* is the South. Let it be divided into two parts, so that two stones are made from it. Take the stone that was at the North and place it in water so that it floats, and it will be seen that the point *a* remains North. Its nature is not taken away by the break. If you bring the stones together again, you will see they follow the same rule. And according to the part of this stone which was toward the North, it becomes a new South pole at the break. Thus the stone of which we spoke, in figure *a b*, is joined to the remainder...

## Refutation of a certain opinion
### regarding the magnet

**S**ome weak-minded investigators <note>original: "debiles mensitatores"</note> have imagined that the cause by which the magnet acts exists in the mineral locations where veins of magnets are found. Whence they say that it moves toward the poles of the world <term>polos mundi</term> <note>the celestial poles around which the heavens rotate</note> only because of the multitude of stones situated in those parts.
But these people are ignorant of the fact that this stone is found in diverse parts of the world; therefore, the stone would move toward those diverse places of the world [if their theory were true], which is false. Likewise, the locations under the poles would not suffice for this, since they are uninhabitable.

...because that [influence] is shared by many things. It is from that place that the movement of the magnet is directed toward us. This force compels it, not only from the north but also from the south. The stone's power does not come from iron mines <note>original: "minis ferri"</note> but from other parts of the world; the proof of this is that wherever a person may be, they can see with their own eyes that this stone moves according to the position of the sphere of the world. 

All the circles of the world <note>The celestial meridians</note> meet at the poles of the world; therefore, the poles of the magnet receive their influence from the poles of the world. It is clearly apparent from this that the magnet does not point toward the nautical star <note>The North Star, Polaris</note>, for the circles of the world do not meet there, but rather at the poles. The nautical star is found outside the pole of the world's sphere, unless one were in a region where the star appeared directly overhead. 

Therefore, it is clear that the parts of the stone receive their power from the heavens. This influence may be considered a fluid or a likeness of the heavens, which is retained so that it forms not only the poles of the stone from the poles of the world, but the whole stone receives influence and virtue from the whole sky. To test this, I suggest a specific method: 

Round the stone and find the poles in it, as was shown before. Then, arrange the stone upon two sharp pivots <note>original: "stilos acutos"</note> so that one pivot is lightly fixed into each pole of the stone, allowing the stone to move upon them without any difficulty. Once this is done,

One of the poles should be elevated and the other depressed, according to the elevation and depression of the poles of the heavens in the region where you are. 

If the stone then moves by its own natural motion, you should rejoice, for you have reached the goal of creating a "perpetual motion" machine <note>Peregrinus believed that a perfectly balanced spherical magnet, aligned with the earth's axis, would rotate once every 24 hours in sympathy with the heavens</note>. By this instrument, you will be saved from all manual labor <note>Meaning the labor of manual astronomical calculations</note>. # Another instrument for finding the aforementioned altitudes of the stars

Another instrument for finding the aforementioned **altitudes of the stars** consists of three flat rulers made of wood, iron, or copper. These must be strong and rigid so that they cannot be easily bent or twisted; they should be four-sided and simple. A line should be drawn through the middle of their faces along their length and in the center of their width. These rulers will be designated **f**, **g**, and **h**.

The line **f g** is marked with **h** at a specific point on the ruler. Regarding the joints or plates <note>original: "finturas uel plaquas"</note>, the longer the ruler is, the better. Its remainder, **g h**, acts as the "tail of the stone" <note>original: "cauda lapidis," likely referring to a base or counterweight</note> or is taken as the base from which the viewer observes from **e** to **d**, so that you may fix the eye upon it.

On the other ruler, there should be two equal sighting vanes <term>original: "pinule," small plates with holes used for lining up a star</term>, and you shall make them in the manner of the two vanes of an **astrolabe** <note>a portable instrument used by astronomers and navigators to measure the altitude of celestial bodies</note>. They should be positioned so that their two middle lines are erect above the middle line **f l**. In the middle of these vanes, there should be two opposing holes at an equal distance from the line **f l**. One should be placed at point **f** and the other at point **l**. These two parts will be joined together with a square pivot <note>original: "quadrapolo"</note> so that the ruler **l f** can be moved upward or downward. They should be fixed at one foot <note>referring to a pivot point</note>, yet able to move further from or closer to the other ruler. Then, the ruler **h m** and the line **h k** should be carefully marked on both of those two lines **f**...

<column-break/>

<margin>LL</margin>
...**h** and **f l** with a cord. Divide its lengths **h f l m** into equal parts, and according to any one of these sections, divide the rest. If you are able, divide the remainder of the line **h m** according to the same scale, so that in that case, you may divide it into as many parts as you wish. This is done so that the measurement of the chords of the arc <note>original: "mete corde arcus," a geometric method to determine angles by measuring the straight-line distance between two points on a circle</note> in degrees does not exceed a certain quantity.

Through **h**, along the two paths **f g** and **h m**, pierce two round and equal holes in the likeness of sighting vanes. Fix them to the poles—specifically the poles of the iron **astrolabe**—so that the ruler **h m** can move upward and downward like a foot. Then, across its middle width in the upper part, from the extremity in the straight-line portion toward the angle, draw a line to the middle line we mentioned. In a similar way, from **f l** at the furthest extremity, through an exterior hole, the height and width of the ruler **h m** are set so that its alignment is not lost, just as in linear scales.

The line **h m** is placed upon a flat zone. Then, the base **a b c d**, upon which **f h g** is set, is adjusted until the line **f c** stands exactly upon the **meridian line** <note>the north-south line indicating noon</note>. This is verified by a **plumb line** <term>original: "perpendicularem," a weight on a string used to find a true vertical</term> erected from here through **l**. If you suspend the plumb line from the upper point to point **h**, you will know by this vertical line whether it is correctly upright above the base **a b c d**, and consequently above the lines of the remaining section.

# ->Prologue on the Construction of the Sphere<-

**S**ince the foundations of solid astronomy <term>astrologia: in this context, the term refers to the scientific study of the stars (astronomy) rather than modern horoscopic astrology</term> and of theoretical contemplation are uniquely strengthened by their subtleties and inexhaustible depth, let us touch upon those things which are specific to its name. Above this same natural science, among all professors of this discipline, the **astronomical instrument** has held a position where it leaves no path for understanding the movements of the celestial bodies and the heavens unexplored. However, although this instrument, in its many parts, may seem to involve four things—namely, the agreement by which they are moved in relation to one another, and toward our own operations which lead us into the work of the days—it may perhaps be a sign of gratitude that we, or our friends among the Indian philosophers, mark these examples. For example, the planets can be clearly figured in spheres, and the spheres within them. One instrument is more primary than another, as was known to every philosopher and in the **Almagest** <note>The *Almagest* is the 2nd-century mathematical and astronomical treatise on the motions of stars and planetary paths by Claudius Ptolemy.</note> of this author, who first fabricated the **armillary instrument** <note>original: "instrūmētū armillatū"; a model of objects in the sky consisting of a spherical framework of rings</note> through his own subtlety. Nor did he, like those the common people call "shapers," merely figure it on a sphere, but rather he found a more open way to show the daily configurations of the heaven from its depths. He invented the **astrolabe** of this Ptolemy according to the likeness of the image of the sphere, but in another mode and form. For one must imagine the sphere as if it were flat and stretched out <term>planisphere: the projection of a 3D sphere onto a 2D plane</term>, in which, although it is demonstrated by subtle geometric proofs, the author appears to be effective both in the imagination of the parts and in the thing itself, where it seems difficult because of the oblique

<column-break/>

angles that must be imagined. Nor by such ingenuity, even if described on the bottom part, is the cause of them lost—that is, because they do not meet at different heads in the diameter or in concavity, but rather from custom; and it is seen, though not considered a plain, from the latitudes in a manner that is difficult and almost impossible. I say that some may be deceived in their prior thoughts, thinking that certain plectra <note>mechanical parts or indicators</note> are above, as if they were drawn underneath and leveled, or rather more equally balanced. And in this age of the ancients, they come to this instance, for many see the utility of the astrolabe under such a quantity—not as if it were easy to taste for the listener, but as something diligently and better approved, as is said of Ptolemy's <margin>A</margin> great instruments. Through these, only the stars are perceived in longitude and latitude, and the figure in it is an imagination, though the galaxy <note>The Milky Way</note>, etc., can be known in the sphere by its own power, namely regarding the daily motions. At first it was not possible, however, to have the construction and volumes of the astrolabe as it had been handed down from the ancients to any person. But whatever we may say regarding the construction and utility of the instrument—that is, the solid sphere or the astrolabe—let the eloquence of God open it to us. We, moved by the author's purpose, for the utility of those who wish to listen to this treatise on the sphere, first set down the arrangement of this instrument. And diligently, through the final parts, let the treatise speak of its utility. Indeed, the construction of this instrument is easy to see and very delightful, and its utility is highly desirable among those who know the foundations and models of astronomy. There are two ways for these instruments: that which is made for the sphere, and the wheel, and others in perfection.
<margin>IV</margin>

### Since the method of proposing [the construction] 49

Since, therefore, holy God willed the instrument to be set forth, you should first make a ball <term>pila: a solid sphere or globe</term> of metal or of solid wood with smooth surfaces. First <unclear>measure</unclear> it with feet <note>likely measuring dividers or a stand</note> or prepare it. To make this ball, take a piece of solid wood and hew it with an ax, then reduce it to a spherical shape as you wish to carry it. Afterwards, find in it two opposite points for the **poles** <note>the North and South celestial poles</note>. While moving it through those points, it becomes a turned object on a **lathe** <term>tornus: a machine tool used to rotate a workpiece to perform various operations such as cutting and sanding</term>. Likewise, you should pour your effort into those two points to refine the whole instrument for the student. From that ball, the method of turning the ball should not be a burden to you. From this, the ball is finished, for that ball is truly formed into a sphere.

Next, you shall place the ring over another point on the sphere, and with the sphere itself in its frame, you shall mark with the point of the knife a circle along the meridian ring; this shall be the **colure of the solstices** <note>the circle passing through the celestial poles and the solstices</note>.

By rotating the sphere at an equal distance from the equinoctial, you shall describe a circle with the point of the knife.

## Part Two, Section 1: On the general utility of this hemisphere in its own right

After, with God's help, the first part of this work—concerning the explanation of the **hemisphere** <term>hemisphere: here referring to a planispheric representation of the celestial or terrestrial globe on a flat surface</term> and the circles established above by our pen—has been completed, we now turn to the manner of its power and utility, or its benefits. Some of these are very general and some are specific. One general utility is that through this hemisphere, one may have knowledge of the [celestial] poles, the description of the world, and the two parallel lines for the **Zodiac** <term>Zodiac: the belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs, marking the path of the sun, moon, and planets</term>, and the two remaining circles for the **Arctic** and **Antarctic**. We shall also speak of the five **zones** <term>zones: the five broad subdivisions of Earth's surface based on climate and latitude</term> of the world, which were mentioned above. 

Moving from the pole toward the **Arctic Circle**, there is a space called the **frigid** or **frozen zone** <note>original: *zona frigida vel congelata*</note>. In this part of the world, very few people dwell, or rather it is barely inhabited, because of the extreme cold, since it is located so close to the pole where the cold is sharp and constant, as is known by the wise. There, no animal can easily live that possesses the spark of reason or power. 

The space that exists between the Arctic Circle and the **Circle of Cancer** <note>The Tropic of Cancer</note> is called the **temperate zone** <note>original: *zona temperata*</note>, which is for the most part inhabited. The space between the **Circle of Capricorn** <note>The Tropic of Capricorn</note> and the **Antarctic Circle** is likewise a temperate zone. Beyond the **equinoctial** <note>the Equator</note> line, the space enclosed between it and the Antarctic Circle is also called a frigid or frozen zone, similar to the first one, because of its coldness and the few people who dwell there. It also appears that in this hemisphere, the circle is clearly shown which the Sun describes by its own motion, which is called the Zodiac according to its latitude. This is distinguished according to the signs... <unclear>of the stars</unclear>... 

<column-break/>

...the values of these things are shown according to the manner in which they are properly made. Here you have all the stars according to their magnitude and the figures of the constellations, and the images of the celestial bodies. These are positioned just as they are found in the heavens, placed by their positions according to their proper order... <note>The text describes how the stars are plotted onto the instrument to mirror the night sky</note> through the meridian lines... and by turning the thread toward the south and north, the parallels appear through the instrument. Thus, one may have knowledge of all the stars, both the fixed stars and the others... and the movement which is called the direct motion... as shown above. The thread shows which stars rise and set, and according to which signs of the zodiac they are aligned... as we shall see in the following utilities.

### Chapter 2: On the adaptation of the hemisphere to any region

It is necessary to adapt the structure of the hemisphere to your **latitude** <term>latitude: the angular distance of a place north or south of the earth's equator</term>. On the meridian line, compute the degrees from the pole according to the latitude of your region. Then, move the corresponding part... of the cords... through the holes, and place the thread over the meridian line with the space... <unclear>of the miles</unclear>... from the top.

### For obtaining the figure of heaven
<note>The "figure of heaven" (figura coeli) refers to a horoscope or a map showing the positions of the celestial bodies and the twelve houses at a specific moment.</note>

The 12 houses are found through the astrolabe in the evening, and at dawn through the stars at night; if you wish to take the altitude of any star known to you through the **alidade** <term>alidade: the revolving pointer on an astronomical instrument used for sighting a star and reading its angle</term> and it has moved in the said day, place the fourth part of the alidade upon the star in my part in which the star was, such as in the line of the midheaven, or because of the axis of the star in the fourth of the angles, until that same star lies under the fourth of the wings [of the instrument]. Then, under the aforesaid steps you have taken, proceed; then, from the degrees placed, consider how with both 30 degrees in the 9th it was in the said **horizon** <term>horizon: the circle where the sky meets the earth</term> at night, so that the degree which hangs at the end of the 9th degree, or in the said horizon in the west, just like the rising degree. Do this in the said rising; then, if it was under that shadow, it is that which feeds the midday, the 10th house, the **nadir** <term>nadir: the point on the celestial sphere directly opposite a given position; here, the point 180 degrees from a specific house or the sun</term>, or the sign in the angle of the earth, which is the 4th house. Find the remaining houses in the manner described at the beginning of the book of signs.

---

### To know the dawn or twilight

If you wish to know the arrangement, follow the measurements as has already been said, using the immovable part. The degree is either of the sun or the sun's position above the nadir, and because of the degrees in the fourth of the wings which are from the true nadir of the sun even unto the horizon; for example, if it were 18 [degrees] <note>18 degrees is the standard astronomical measure for the sun's position below the horizon to define the start of dawn or the end of twilight</note>, then the nadir of the sun is below the western part and it is the meridian of dawn, and the sun is approaching with its rays. And if the nadir of the sun was toward the east, it is the end of the evening **twilight** <note>original: *epustuli*, likely a scribal error or variant for *crepusculi*</note> and the failing of the sun's rays. If indeed the degrees are more than 18, the evening **twilight** <note>original: *epustulu(m)*</note> has passed, if the nadir of the sun is toward the east, or the dawn has not yet begun

<sig>B iij</sig>

<column-break/>

if they are toward the west. If the aforesaid were fewer than 18, the evening twilight is not yet finished; then, according to what has passed, if it was used to lead the nadir of the sun, either it has already passed for the dawn, if it was from its nadir toward the heat [the east], but otherwise the twilight remains for the dawn. Thus it is said: place the nadir of the sun as 18 [degrees] are in the fourth of the wings, then at the boundary, and the head suspended in the meridian through its own [line], place the nadir of the sun on the horizon and make a mark in it... after having it as in every [equi]noctial, from its own mark in the fourth of the meridian, divide that by 15 <note>Dividing by 15 converts degrees of arc into equal hours, as the sky rotates 15 degrees every hour.</note>, which results in equal hours; and what remains when multiplied by 15, you have as parts of an hour. For so many hours and such a part of an hour shall the evening twilight or the dawn last, or the twilight is nearly equal.

And those which are my marks have lost the western pole, or the head... the sun is elongated from them and again toward the parts... 30 you wish then... of two places... the fixed stars at the **zenith** <term>zenith: the point in the sky directly above the observer</term> in the universe.

### Chapter VI: On Measurements

For everyone desiring to know the true height of any elevated thing, let him begin the mystery through the **ring** <note>likely the thumb-ring or suspension ring of the astrolabe</note> and turn the meridian cord toward the part of the thing's height above the plane of the horizon.

<column-break/>

[The observer should hold] the cord for all purposes toward the elevated object and you shall elevate the **sighting rule** <term>sighting rule: the alidade or pointer used to sight objects</term> through which the [eye] aims toward the upper limit... always through the elevated sighting rule... so that the limit can be seen... through which points the cord [falls]... by looking at the appearance of the height.

If it falls upon the **points** <note>This refers to the "Shadow Square" on the back of the astrolabe, usually divided into 12 units or "points"</note> exactly, and the height of the object equals the distance measured from the feet of the object to the line of the triangle where you are standing, from your appearance [position] up to the eye.

If indeed the points are more than 12, then the height of the object will be greater than the distance measured from the feet of the object with your standing position; then, however many points there are more than 12, such will be the proportion of the height of the object to the measured distance... just as the proportion of points upon which the sighting rule falls is to 12.

If the points are fewer than 12, then the height of the object is less than the distance measured from the feet of the object with your standing position; then, however many points are fewer than 12, the proportion of the height of the object to the measured distance from the feet of the object is as the proportion of points to 12.

If however you wish to know by the distance of the points what is seen... such as in feet or palms, so for the measurement of the object... [calculate] the feet or palms by the proportion... to the denoted points or feet or palms... If therefore the points... found were 12, the height of the object is the total distance in feet or palms that you measured. If the points were more or fewer than 12... [divide] by 12 and what comes out [is the result].
