# Here Begins the Treatise on the Semissa

Because not everyone is called to our study of **philosophy** <term>philosophy: in this context, the study of natural science and astronomy</term>, nor do they all pursue **philosophy** <term>philosophy: likely a scribal repetition or emphasis</term> itself—some through negligence, others shunning the harsh and tedious difficulties and the length of time required—it is necessary to set forth <unclear>and rehearse</unclear> a more clearly defined work regarding the movement of the world and its quality <term>mozis: likely a contraction for "motus," meaning motion</term>. Therefore, I intend to expedite in these writings a certain measure <note>original: "mensuram"</note>—composed with God's help—through which the true locations of all the planets may easily be found without the use of <unclear>laborious</unclear> tables, the operations of which are most tedious to the mind.

## How this instrument is intended to be constructed

Take two equal **radii** <term>semidiametros: the radius of a circle</term> of a circular figure which is called the **Semissa** <note>The "Semissa" or "Semissis" is an astronomical instrument, its name implying it is based on a semicircle or half-unit</note>. One part is for all the planets, and the other part is for all the **epicycles** <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used to explain planetary orbits</term>. And let the diameter of the Semissa be the space *a c d*. And let the <unclear>diameter</unclear> be *a c b* in its place upon point *c*, which point is placed in the middle of the diameter *a c b*, as is the center of the earth. Divide this diameter *a c b* into 180 equal parts. Then, divide the parts *a c* and *b c* into 180 equal parts, which will be the degrees of the figures. From there, divide each <unclear>division</unclear> into 60 parts, and again divide each of those into parts which will be the degrees of the figures. Place the appropriate markings for the divisions of the figures every ten degrees.

<column-break/>

...of the **deferent** <term>deferent: the main orbital circle in Ptolemaic astronomy</term> in the figure concerning the construction, etc.

Let there be placed in the construction a certain very thin rule in the manner of a **volvelle** <term>volvelle: a rotating paper or metal disc used as a calculating device</term>; in its assembly, let there be a **fiducial line** <term>linea fiducie: a straight edge or line used for sighting and alignment</term> *d f*, which is the radius of the **deferent** of all the planets. Let the line *a d* be the longest radius... serving the radius of the Semissa. Let there be a point called *q* at the head of the **volvelle** for the structure of all the points and the rules of all the **epicycles**. This is the center of all the deferents. Afterward, place the points *d* and *m* as two very short lines... according to the nature of the tables... upon the face of the volvelle. Then, divide the line *d f* (or another of equal length) into 60 equal parts. These parts represent the distance of the centers of the deferents of the planets and the magnitudes of the **epicycles** <term>epicictorz: scribal variant of epicyclorum</term>. You will find these centers and the sizes of the epicycles in the following tables: *Concerning the distances of centers and the sizes of epicycles* <note>original: "De distantiis centr̃z x magnitu dinib’ epycictoy"</note>, which have been extracted from another source. Let a line equal to line *d f*, divided into 60 parts, be placed in each Semissa in the **model** <term>exemplari: the master drawing or template</term> of line *d f*. Whenever you wish to calculate the equation, take from the table the corresponding distance of the centers. Extende the feet of the compass upon the points of the volvelle... between these feet are contained the quantity of the prescribed measure.

### On the Calculation of Mean Motions

Since arguments are found regarding motion and the <term>computus</term> <note>The science of calculating time, calendars, and astronomical cycles</note> etc., the proper method is the application of their changes, and the other mean motions as they are found through the tables of such matters, etc. When you wish to find the point of such a motion, look in the table of **collected years** <note>Medieval tables grouped years (often in blocks of 20 or 28) to simplify long-term calculations</note> for the accumulated years that you desire. If you do not find that exact number of years, take the next closest value that is less than your number. Then, take what you find written there in **degrees**, **minutes**, etc., and write them down individually in the order they appear in the table. 

Then, take the remaining years that were left over from the "collected years" and look for them in the table of **expanded years**. You will find figures given in **signs**, **degrees**, **minutes**, and **seconds**. Place these under the first set: signs under signs, degrees under degrees, minutes under minutes, and seconds under seconds. Similarly, note the points you find for the months. See how many days of the month have passed and enter the table of days; write down what you find there—degrees, minutes, seconds, etc.—and add them to the others. 

Because the day begins at the midpoint of the preceding day <note>Astronomical days traditionally began at noon rather than midnight</note>, see how many hours have passed since the preceding day and enter the same table of hours. Place what you find under the others in the same way, with minutes and seconds. Then, from the table of minutes, place what you find under the others as before. If there are 30 or more minutes, you may carry them over as a whole unit. You can then collect the fractions into a whole by dividing by 60; as many times as sixty goes into the sum, add that many minutes to the next column.

<column-break/>

Whatever remains should be placed by itself. Likewise, for the minutes, let a total be made properly. For however much time has passed, add that many degrees for the days, and whatever sum remains in the hours, place it in the column for degrees. Divide the minutes and seconds by 30, and whatever that yields, add it to the signs. The signs, degrees, minutes, and seconds that remain should then be placed below the values previously calculated. When the sum is produced, the result that remains in degrees, minutes, and seconds in the preceding place will be the **mean motion** <note>The theoretical position of a planet if it moved at a constant speed in a perfect circle</note> for the present hour according to the **years of Toulouse** <note>Refers to the 'Tables of Toulouse,' a set of astronomical data adapted for the longitude of that city</note>.

If, however, you wish to find the mean motion for another longitude <note>Geographic distance east or west</note>, you must consider how many hours of longitude that place is before or after a reference point like Toulouse. If the place is in the **East** in relation to Toulouse, add the difference to the mean motion found for Toulouse. If it is in the **West**, subtract it from the same. What then remains will be the mean motion for that desired place, adjusted for the difference in longitude and hour. 

This is called the "mean motion at the equal hour," which leads to the "equalized mean motion" of the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note>. You will then arrive at the distance of the body itself from its mean apogee, equated by signs, minutes, and seconds. This calculation shows the position where the mean motion is equalized, as will be clear in the following sections.

### On the Calculation of the Argument and the Apogee

Likewise, a **superior planet** <note>The planets further from the Sun than Earth: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> then has one [argument] found by subtracting the **mean motion** <note>The average speed of a planet, as if it moved in a perfect circle</note> of the body from the **mean motion of the Sun**. The remainder is the **certain argument** of the body. This is because whatever body is in a certain mean motion at any time—whether in the time of the mean motion of the Sun or now—that body is, according to you, in the **mean apogee** <note>Latin: *aux media*; the point in a planet's orbit furthest from the Earth</note> according to the **epicycle** <term>epicycle: a small circle on which a planet moves, while the center of that circle moves along a larger circle called the deferent</term>. And the fourth part of the time of the mean motion of the Sun adds the arc of the mean motion of the epicycle by the side of the elongation; then the body of that same planet is at a distance from the mean apogee according to the epicycle.

**B**y what was said before, it is clear that during the time of the said motion of the argument, a planet moved in another time not mentioned. Subtract the mean motion of that planet from the mean motion of the Sun at noon, and the remainder is the motion of the **mean argument** of that same planet at the said time. You have held, however, the **mean apogee** in the **eighth sphere** <note>The sphere of the fixed stars, which medieval astronomers believed moved slowly over time due to the precession of the equinoxes</note> at a distance in the time of the mean motion of the planets from the place of the first apogee, or the **deferent** <note>The path carrying the epicycle</note>, and by its own motion measured by a sign. But the distance of the Sun is from the solar argument and not from the true spaces; however, the distance of the apogee of the planet—which is called the <unclear>m</unclear> **examiner** <note>Possibly a reference to an *examinator*, a tool or table for verifying calculations</note>—verifies the locations of the planet through tables according to the space in the said time of mean motion, truly 30 and <unclear>mu d</unclear>. **W**ith the time of the arc of the said mean distance, there are times of the arc of 30 that are equated <unclear>et a r</unclear> because the arc of the same <unclear>e d</unclear> mean is held.

**J**ust as it is in time, when you have therefore subtracted the apogee in the eighth sphere in the time of the planet from the mean motion of that same planet, the remainder is the **certain argument** of that planet. ...by the motion of the sun, etc., by a fitting ratio. When you are giving the fractions of the signs <note>The zodiac is divided into 12 "signs" of 30 degrees each</note> by taking away the number from the whole light, subtract the **mean motion** <note>The theoretical average speed of a celestial body</note> of the sun from the mean motion of the moon. By doubling the remainder, and with the true mean of the moon, you find that the doubling is indeed the mean of the moon. Then, on account of the mean motion of the sun, you should subtract the motion of the moon; then add the fraction because the mean motion of the moon, which is the sign, is given. And having the **mean apogee** <note>original: *augm medio*; the point furthest from Earth</note> of the sun, one has the true mean of **Venus** and **Mercury**. This is because the mean motion of Venus and Mercury is the same as that of the sun.

**I**t follows that if there is a deficit in the equated apogee of Venus, and therefore the same argument of the sun precedes the mean apogee of Venus, then for the equated apogee of Mercury, the deficit is not noted. This is because the motion of the sun is clearly related to the motion of Mercury. Thus, for the apogee of Mercury, which is greater than the apogee of Venus, the sun is indeed near this value. The sun is not the mean apogee of Mercury, and therefore one must subtract the distance by which the equated apogee of Venus and the equated apogee of Mercury differ. Just as with the mean of Venus, the remainder is the apogee; and for the mean of Mercury, you then add that distance to the mean. If you cannot subtract the apogee, add 12 signs to it. If you add that distance to the mean, subtract it, and the remainder will be the position of Mercury. This is to be observed as a rule: whenever a subtraction is required from a smaller number, 12 signs must be added to the prior number.

<column-break/>

...from the whole, subtract the portion to be taken away. This distance between the apogees of these planets is plain from the tables of Venus and Mercury, which is: **9 signs, 39 minutes, and 41 seconds** <note>original: "9 g g 39 mi ta 41 m"</note>. From the degree of this distance, starting from the apogee of Venus and following the aforementioned fractions of the signs—namely toward the apogee of Mercury—the whole is divided.

**I**t appears that for the motion of the moon and the <term>inferior planets</term> <note>Venus and Mercury, whose orbits are inside Earth's</note>, as well as the center of the sun, the calculation is as follows: When the motion is in any operation, say how much is the mean motion of the apogee; in the composition, say how much is the mean motion of Venus; in the motion, say how much is the mean motion of the sun in a day. Because in the same way, the mean motion of Venus in a day is the same as the mean motion of the sun. The mean motion of Mercury is the motion in a day of the moon, and it is as much as its mean motion doubled, then diminished by twice the mean motion of the sun in a day. If you subtract twice the mean motion of the sun in a day from twice the mean motion of the moon in a day, you will have the doubling mentioned before.

**T**hese mean motions of the planets are to be taken from the tables. However, you must compare them because they are moved in those tables by numbers given to us in years, months, and days. The mean motion of the sun, Mars, and the others are gathered together. If any are omitted, they are distributed proportionately. And if you judge the motion to be different from the mean motions placed in the table, it is because the **radius** <note>The distance from the center of the deferent to the planet</note>...

# The Nocturnal and the Measurement of Night Hours

In the **nocturnal** <note>original: *spera noctis*; literally "sphere of the night," an instrument used to determine the time at night based on the positions of certain stars</note> there is a certain **round plate** <note>original: *tabula rotunda*</note> which is divided into 12 equal parts, in which are written the 12 months, namely January, February, and so on. Below these months are written the lengths of the night—that is, how many hours the night has at its midpoint, and from the middle to the end. And if all the hours are of the greatest value, they will be worth half an hour; each of the first **perforations** <note>original: *foraminibʒ*; holes in the instrument used for alignment or marking</note> which represent the months themselves is worth 30 days. And the other holes, which are marked below, signify the 24 hours of the day; the space existing between two holes is worth one hour. 

To find the hours of the night through this space, it is necessary for the one observing the night to look at the **celestial pole** <note>original: *polū mūdi*</note>, which sailors call the **Star of the Sea** <note>original: *stellā maris*; the North Star or Polaris</note>. By this, the **horologe** <note>original: *horologiū*; a time-keeping device</note> is known, along with two other stars that follow its motion; thus, they call these two stars the **Two Brothers** <note>Refers to the Guards of the Little Dipper (Beta and Gamma Ursae Minoris)</note>. One recognizes the pole in relation to the seven clear stars that shine <note>Likely referring to Ursa Major, the Big Dipper</note>. And between those seven... <unclear>rote</unclear> ...by the Two Brothers, which are the two stars brighter and closer to the pole among those seven stars; the brighter one is more useful for our purpose. Note that the hole which is in the middle of the sphere signifies the celestial pole, and the **volvelle** <note>original: *voluclla*; a movable parchment or metal disk</note> is made for the brighter star of the Two Brothers. For by that star, the pole is moved, just as the volvelle moves with the hole. And when the sphere is positioned... in whatever time...

<column-break/>

This is the method for taking the hours of the night: first, take the month in which you are, as mentioned above, and place a mark in the hole signifying the day in which you are. This mark will represent the middle of the night for the start of the day. See on the sphere how many hours the night previously had, and divide those into two equal parts; place one half to the right and the other to the right and the other to the left, beginning from the mark representing the month of the night. To find the hours you seek, you should then place some mark... adding the other part of the hours... from the mark of the month of the night... placing a mark at the end of the night.

For example, let one place the volvelle at the month of November, and place it where the mark figures the middle of the night. Then, see how many hours the night has; if it has 12, divide them into two equal parts, which are 6 and 6. Count 6 hours on the sphere toward the left from the mark of the month of the night, and place a mark; then count 6 hours toward the right, and there place a mark which shall be the end of the night. You shall do this for every month. If, however, the hours were equal, such as 12 or 14, divide them... so that October is below and September is above... the pole of the sphere in the middle hole of the sphere, namely the sea...

# Here begins the explanation of the Mirror of the Planets by Master John of Lignères

In the name of God, the Merciful, Amen. To satisfy the desire of those studying **astronomy** <term>astronomy: in the Middle Ages, this often included both the calculation of celestial movements and their astrological interpretation</term> and the **sphere** <note>original: *sphaera*; referring to the celestial sphere or the standard textbook *De sphaera mundi*</note>, for anyone of even modest skill in astronomy, many names are given above... demonstrating a method through an instrument in which you will see clearly, as if in a **mirror** <note>original: *speculo*; the "Mirror of the Planets" was a type of equatorium, a mechanical computing device</note>, all the movements of the planets and finally the location of the **dragon** <term>dragon: the "Caput" and "Cauda Draconis," or the lunar nodes where the moon's path intersects the ecliptic</term> in the **ninth sphere** <note>original: *nona sphaera*; in medieval cosmology, the sphere beyond the fixed stars that provides the daily rotation of the universe</note>.

By revolving this, one finds the location, movement, and slowness of the celestial bodies, which are consulted at all times, namely the **dignities** <term>dignities: the varying degrees of influence a planet holds based on its position in the zodiac</term> and many other things. Thus, without needing **astronomical tables** <term>tables: complex grids of numbers, like the Alfonsine Tables, usually required to calculate planetary positions</term> of the movements of the planets, one may obtain the data through the Mirror of the Planets much more quickly. This work is divided into three parts: The first touches upon the most refined method of construction, in which this mirror is briefly described. The second truly treats the most fragrant proportions <note>original: *ora*; likely referring to the mathematical ratios or 'orders'</note> for the completion of this mirror. The third indeed shows most sweetly how this mirror is to be revolved and clearly praised.

## The construction of this instrument

<meta>This page continues the instructions for constructing the "Mirror of the Planets," an equatorium designed by John of Lignères. There are 22 circles which, when drawn as one, produce 22 spaces. Of these, one upper space contains the markings for the **Sun and Moon** <note>original: *solo sol et lunc*</note> only; and for the other two planets, there are then two spaces. Above all these, the first space leads with it through which the certain movement of the Moon is found, as well as **Venus** <note>original: *vcils*; likely a contraction for Venus</note> and the **Dragon's Head** <term>Dragon's Head: the ascending lunar node, where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic</term>...

Then, where the spaces are immediately adjacent for the aforementioned or for the other planets, they should be arranged in this order in the upper spaces: first the highest planets, then the lower ones, through which the **attained movement** <note>original: *dem matus*</note> for the future is found. Each of these spaces is then distributed in order below. # Here begins the second treatise
## on the visualization of the sphere, etc. <note>original: "de ymaginatione spere et c"</note>

Indeed, many astrological <note>In the medieval period, "astrology" and "astronomy" were often used interchangeably to describe the study of the stars.</note> matters must be understood by us through this mental visualization before we attempt to construct a solid body or a void defined by drawn circles. These circles, which are constructed through the mathematical division of three-dimensional bodies, are formed according to the nature of the world. At its center, we should perceive something indissoluble in comparison to the vastness of the world, just as we understand the world itself to be immovable, while everything within it moves according to our visualization. 

Thus, presiding over this visualization, let us understand the entire surface of the world to be taken in every part, both the eastern and western, as much in its half-circles as in its flat planes. We visualize one half to be beneath our feet and beneath every body, and the other half above the world. We imagine a certain cord <note>Latin: "corda," referring here to a geometric line or chord</note> extending from the eastern point to the western point, and another from the north to the south. A third extends toward its opposite point beneath our feet, as is clearly evident.

Therefore, we shall understand that such an eastern point is formed by a path that leads to the western point and returns through the opposite side beneath our feet to the west. This circle is called the **equator of the day** <note>The celestial equator</note> or the *equidistant circle*. There is also another circle passing through the point of the south and its opposite, and through the two vertices above the head <note>The zenith and nadir</note>; this is called the **meridian** or the *circle of midday*. Furthermore, there is our meridian through the vertex <unclear>c</unclear> passing through the [east] and west, which is then called the **horizon** or the circle [of the boundary].

<column-break/>

[This circle] is sent forth between those three cords. Within these three lies the <term>vapor</term> <note>Likely referring to the atmosphere or the "sublunary" region near the earth</note> just as on the earth itself. Through our two axes of midday—the equinoctial or equidistant circles—and at the peak of the <term>antorthia</term> <note>original: "antorthia"; likely a corruption of "Antarctic" or referring to the opposing polar heights</note>, are what they call the **poles**. For astrologers have said, or define, that the poles are the common ends of the axis; an indivisible cord that goes through the axis of the world and the circle. These common cords are similarly those where the [west] and the [cardinal points] are called the poles of the circles of the world. 

The cord, however, that goes from the vertex to its opposite point beneath our feet is called the **axis**, and the poles are common to each of these. Thus, it is said that in the circle of the hours, the world is turned, and its body <unclear>??</unclear> is a great or "greater" circle. Indeed, any great circle's axis passes through the center of the world. Great circles are also larger than the span of mid-day, dividing it into two equal parts through themselves. 

Of these circles, however, one exists without a "yoke" <note>original: "sine iug[um]"; possibly meaning without a pair or being unique in its function</note> or by its own nature in the meridian part, dividing the world into four parts because they [the quadrants] divide it. These do not have circles that are as unique to one another as they are to our body or to us, and they divide the earth into parts. Just as there are axes, so too is the visualization between the equinoctial circle and the pole at the vertex. Regarding the equidistant circles, which are inserted through the middle of the world-circle, they are said to be from a point above the earth and likewise from an opposite point beneath the earth. They lead from the proper meridian point, moving from the horizon to the opposite point. 

Likewise, one should understand how [one moves] from the equinox to the pole of our vertices. These circles are arranged according to their comprehension from the equinox to the pole of the world-vertex. From where, then, do we [derive] these circles?

<meta>This page continues the technical geometric visualization of the celestial sphere. Having previously established the "equator of the day," the text now details how the size of celestial circles varies relative to the poles and introduces the coordinate systems of the horizon, including almucantars (altitude) and azimuth (bearing), concluding with the introduction of the zodiac.</meta>

It is said that the closer these circles are to the pole, the smaller they are, and the further away they are, the larger they are. Or, it may be understood that a large circle is perceived in a small space, since it is separated by 360 degrees through larger degrees than if they were seen through smaller circles. **For example** <note>original: "Verbi gratia"</note>, you might imagine one hundred of these circles in the height of one hundred degrees; these circles are large even if they are seen in parts. Through the pole of the equinoctial circle <note>the celestial equator</note>, each of them intersects the equinoctial circle at two opposite degrees. These circles are called <term>colures</term> <note>the two principal meridians of the celestial sphere that pass through the poles and the equinoctial/solstitial points</note>. Thus, all the degrees of each of these circles recede from one another, and so toward all the circles equidistant from the equinox. The additional arc which tends from there, by the same arrangement, intersects these equidistant circles toward their poles and toward the eastern and western points of the world, ascending and traversing each arc toward the pole and toward itself. Whenever the <term>meridian</term> circle distinguishes its large polar circles—those equidistant circles which tend toward the south—it thus divides the equidistant circles into 360 degrees. 

The **Horizon** is a circle at an equal distance of degrees between the earth and the sky. Its pole is in the middle of the summit <note>the zenith</note> above a person. The more it ascends and approaches the pole, the smaller the circles become; these are the <term>almucantars</term> <note>original: "almicantarath"; circles of altitude parallel to the horizon</note>. It is said that the almucantars which intersect are parts of the school <note>possibly a reference to a specific diagram or teaching tradition</note> where each of them is distinguished in whole and as if half or anew circles. Without a doubt, the horizon divides its great polar circles, such as the equatorial, and the half of the circle consists of 180 degrees. Around their equidistant parts, they are divided into 360 degrees; thus these circles are called <term>azimuth</term> <note>vertical circles used to measure horizontal bearing</note>. The azimuth of any of those circles is the arc which is from the horizon all the way to the pole, or if from true noon toward the west, it ascends through those almucantar circles.

<column-break/>

One measures through the circle of azimuths and the measurement from the same almucantar. Both azimuth and almucantar are very useful for taking the position of the sun or a star. Through the described almucantar circles, the altitude of the sun or a star is found, according to the degrees elevated above the horizon. However, through the meridian azimuths, its position in the horizon is determined. Thus, the horizontal space is defined by the four primary quarters: the first, which is from the east to the south, is called the south-eastern; the second is from the south to the west, and is called the south-western; the third is from the west to the north, and is called the north-western; the fourth is the north-eastern. 

According to this, and with the aforementioned, the first is that through which the great circle is divided according to the meridians into equal halves. Through another circle, as has already been said, there is no doubt between them. This orthogonal <note>right-angled</note> measurement, which the arc contains, renders the true measurement. According to the orthogonal, it gives an equal measurement because it is an oblique arc of a circle. In the meridian circle, there are two points which are the <term>solstices</term> <note>original: "solsticia"</note>. One is understood from the noon above, which is distant from the equator by 24 degrees <note>The medieval measurement for the obliquity of the ecliptic, usually rounded from approximately 23.5 degrees</note>. The other indeed is from the north <note>original: "a n." likely for "a nocte" or "a boreas"</note> under that distance which is 24 degrees from the equator. According to these two points, and through the west, a certain path <unclear>comes</unclear> into it, which some call the **Zodiac** <note>original: "zodiacum"</note>, and some in Latin call the **Sign-bearer** <note>original: "signiferum"</note>, and some call the circle of the signs. It contains the imagined forms around the <term>horoscope</term> <note>here referring to the rising point of the ecliptic</note>, or a single degree of form. It intersects the equidistant circle <note>the equator</note> obliquely and is positioned toward its poles.

<meta>This page continues the technical description of the celestial sphere's geometry, moving from the general concept of the horizon and colures to the specific division of the heavens into quadrants and the introduction of the zodiac and its twelve signs.</meta>

That circle which is northern is hidden below the earth, while that which is southern is positioned above the earth. Now, for the sake of understanding the world, these are said to be divided into **quarters**. The first quarter is from the eastern point to the north pole; the second is from that same pole to the western point; the third is from the western point to the south pole; and the fourth is from that pole back to the eastern point. 

Among these, in the meridian of the world, there are equal parts, and thus there are **12 parts** which properly belong to the <term>zodiac</term> <note>the belt of the heavens within which the sun, moon, and planets move</note>. Any figure or division of these is called a **sign**. The first part is called **Aries** <note>the Ram</note>, the second **Taurus** <note>the Bull</note>, the third **Gemini** <note>the Twins</note>, and so on. 

These names of the stars were applied to their respective parts because of certain qualities contained within those parts, so that they might be held to provide firm providence for the disposition of human affairs. Also, these are the 12 parts by which the world is divided, through which the entire zodiac and other circles possess a total of **360 degrees**. 

Through these, one understands two continuous poles here. One is understood from the first meridian and is above the earth, distant from the north pole by 24 degrees and from the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>the celestial equator</note> by 66 degrees. The other indeed is from the south, located below the earth, distant from the southern pole by 24 degrees and from the equinoctial by 66 degrees. 

Therefore, the zodiac itself is a circle which extends from both poles toward the heights. In the three aforementioned parts of the world they are joined; and the quantities of the circles are those which are extended from one pole to the north pole, and on the other side from that same pole to the south pole. The boundaries of these are a point in the circumpolar circles, and even more, they divide the circles of their poles into 180 parts.

<column-break/>

In another way, those which are not distant from the first divide the surrounding circle into 360 parts. To us, therefore, as we divide the time of the world, we gather <unclear>opidit</unclear> through the imaginary lines in the world. We consider time to be immobile and established by the Creator of the world in a strong way. 

We have the aforementioned **chords** <note>straight lines connecting two points on a curve, used here for geometric calculation</note> and primordial things which constitute the body, the axes, and the chords that measure distance. We also have the poles and the <unclear>mu[n]g</unclear> of their poles, which in their appendages have a measure of **360**. 

These measures possess an efficacy on the earth, by which we conduct **astrology** or **astronomy**. Because of our imaginary constructions, we cannot know <unclear>cetate</unclear> clearly, but it is said to relate to the imaginary through <unclear>elipsis</unclear> <note>likely referring to the elliptical path or an eclipse</note>.

# Here begins the preface of the propositions of the following instruments concerning eclipses

To have an easier method and with less labor regarding those things which occur only in eclipses of the sun and moon—namely, the diversity of <term>aspects</term> <note>original: "afspectū," referring to parallax, the apparent displacement of a celestial object when viewed from different locations</note> in longitude and latitude, as well as in other associated boundaries to be calculated, and the magnitudes and durations and other matters pertaining to the whole—I will set forth the mode and form of the composition of two instruments. These instruments possess two faces and are partly derived from the **Albion** <note>a sophisticated astronomical instrument designed by Richard of Wallingford in the 14th century</note> and other models, though the names are changed for this specific construction. At that time, in the first draft and the great heart of the work, it was proposed to have a very easy approach to those things which were previously difficult; specifically, regarding the oppositions of the sun and moon and their eclipses according to their true positions. This is done by calculating the time of the mean lunar opposition and the mean motion of the sun, as well as the mean argument of the moon and the mean argument of the latitude of the moon at that same time.

The first face of the first instrument is primarily useful for the positions of the sun and moon at the time of their mean opposition and for the timing of lunar oppositions in equated days, just as appears in the following instructions. The second face of this instrument is useful for the difference of days between the mean and true oppositions.

The first face of the second instrument is useful for the eclipses of the sun, specifically for the arcs and the parallax in longitude and latitude, and for the entire duration as it is calculated in the Albion. The second face of the second instrument is for obtaining the magnitude and duration of eclipses, which is proposed first.

<column-break/>

Their first forms are distinguished individually from the second, as seen in the figures following the examples.

## Procedure 23: On the lunar eclipse in general and its true magnitude

To have the possible magnitude at that time, look for the position of the moon and the nadir of the sun as if through the sphere of the moon. Then, through this most true time of opposition, determined by the degrees and minutes of the moon, and at that same time through this position of the moon and the nadir of the sun, find the argument of the moon and the argument of the magnitude of the latitude, as was said, through the degrees and minutes of this [position] through the sphere—both for the sun and for the true opposition in <term>equal days: days adjusted for the varying speed of Earth's rotation and orbit</term>—by the degrees and minutes of this, to have the values for the middle of the eclipse.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the Speculum Astronomiae (The Mirror of Astronomy), traditionally attributed to Albertus Magnus. The text establishes a clear boundary between legitimate scientific astronomy and illicit magical practices (necromancy) which were often disguised as astronomical texts in the 13th and 14th centuries.</meta>

# Here begins the treatise of Albertus Magnus on the refutation of books of images and the approval of astronomical books.

On the occasion of certain books, a controversy has arisen among some: those who are truly wise fear the Lord, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the image of the Father and the Wisdom through whom the ages were made. Because the reasoning of these books is suspect to those who love the naked faith, it pleased certain great men that these books—and perhaps their own works, lest they be confused with them—be distinguished from the profession of <term>books of images</term> <note>original: "librorum maginariorum"; these were books of astrological magic or necromancy that used "images" or talismans</note> which has been used as a cloak to trade under the name of astronomy. This has made such works seem weighty to good men and marvelous to all. Therefore, a certain man, a zealot for the faith and for both forms of wisdom <note>referring to both divine theology and natural philosophy</note>, acting in his station, is said to have examined the true contents of these books, separating what is licit from what is illicit, so that the fear of the Almighty may be known.

<margin>
This occurred
</margin>

And all wisdom and reasoning concerning the nature of the stars—with their various shapes and their motion around the poles, the composition of the fixed stars and their paths—is concluded in this figure. It concerns the distance of the <term>equator</term> <note>the great circle of the celestial sphere</note> and the <term>apsides</term> <note>original: "apsisdis"; the points in an orbit farthest from or closest to the center</note> and the position of the spheres and their surfaces.

<column-break/>

...above the apogee of the equator, at which distance the orbits move with the motion of the spheres and the motion of the bodies within those orbits. This includes the paths of the rays, the eclipses of the sun and moon, and the motion in latitude <note>the distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic</note> in their various reflections. These are the orbits and the heights of the sun, both at its rising and its setting, measured by their great magnitude. It treats all the parts of the spheres and the diameters and the magnitude of the bodies of the planets, which can be proven by measurement. We speak of the measurement of these bodies and their diameters, and of the weight and density of these things, which are investigated by our measurements. This includes the various <term>climates</term> <note>original: "chimatuz"; historical geographic zones defined by the length of the longest day</note> and the divisions of the earth, from the middle of the world to the nodes and the equal parts of the horizon.

Furthermore, regarding the diversity of the lengths of days and nights, which arises from the various positions upon the earth, I will explain the differences of the seven climates. These locations are determined by the length of one revolution of the heavens, where in some places the day is longer and in others the night, according to the composition of the celestial bodies.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of legitimate astronomical works. Having established the distinction between licit science and illicit magic on the previous page, the author now lists the foundational texts of the "science of the stars," moving from basic principles of motion to the complex planetary models of Ptolemy and his Arabic commentators.</meta>

...for a long time the sun does not set, nor does it begin another path unless it pertains to the **poles**; and then, in another way, where the whole dignity is made clear by reason. 

Behold, there is one <term>great wisdom</term> <note>original: "magna sapientia"</note> which I have called by the name of **astronomy**. This science is not generated except through those books which are called the books of **geometers** and **arithmeticians** among us. Principally, a book has been set forth concerning this nature which is called the *Universal Gathering of the Sciences* <note>original: "universali gregas ad vclū dūm d̄isciplin̄"; likely referring to Alfraganus’s "Elements of Astronomy"</note>, which begins thus: "The Sphere is said to be..." 

This work is profound and allows no falsehood; there is nothing contrary to the faith except what is taught concerning this science by those with wicked errors. There is also the book of **Ptolemy**, whose praise is great, which is called the *Great Treatise* <note>original: "magafra"; a corruption of the Greek "Megale Syntaxis"</note>, known in Arabic as the **Almagest**. It is a work of even greater perfection, beginning: "It was a good thing..." and it discusses the matter slowly and studiously. 

Next is the book of **Messahalla** <note>an 8th-century Persian-Jewish astronomer</note> concerning the **first motion of the orb**, which begins: "In the name of the Lord..." 

Then there is the work of the Spaniard known as **Albategni** <note>Al-Battani, a 9th-century Arab astronomer</note> in his book which begins: "Among many things..." He shows that certain things have happened over time not through the error of Ptolemy, but through the <term>precession of the stars</term> <note>original: "superpacione radion"; the slow shifting of celestial bodies over centuries</note> discovered by **Hipparchus** <note>original: "abrachis"</note>, which do not seem to conflict with the faith. 

**Johannes** <note>likely John of Seville</note> collected in two books the reasoning of the first book of **Euclid** regarding the measure of the stars, and also the work of **Albategni**, which begins: "While the appearance of things..." but the motion of **Thabit** <note>Thabit ibn Qurra</note> is deceived by the passage of time in his book which begins: "In the greatness of the measure..."

<column-break/>

According to some, **Hipparchus** described the right motions and trends in his books, which are now new among those who have applied themselves to them. <meta>The text continues the previous discussion on the nature of "future possibilities" by examining how they manifest in the human condition—specifically through the lens of poverty, wealth, and the moment of birth (nativity). ## On Providence and the Condition of Birth

Whether among the poor or among the rich, just as "to be" is not governed by a law of equality, so too are some of them led toward **birth** <note>original: "nativitatem"</note>. It is not that they existed previously as matter, but that they were formed. Not every "being" is the same; there is that which is called "eternal being." This power toward birth is determined in time; it is called by a name that "is not," because it exists a great length of time before its actual birth. It is then led toward its own birth, like an artist’s fame <note>original: "famosus art[ifex]"</note> is said to exist before his work is completed.

I say this not of the past, but in the manner of a Master who determines things without the limitations of time. One cannot say "it will never be" of that which is being led toward nature. Perhaps this pertains to the <term>Ingenerate Son</term> <note>A theological term referring to Christ as the "begotten" but eternal Word, often used in debates about how something can be both "born" and "eternal."</note>, a concept often doubted in discussions of **Divine Providence** <note>original: "divina p'uid'z"</note>.

For nothing is better than the works of the Lord. It is nothing other than Divine Providence in these things in which we are present. We are not the cause of these things. There are two paths: one which a person might choose to do, and another which might be chosen differently. In the "Book of Life," <note>original: "libro vividit," likely *libro vitae*</note> these works are seen. If these things were able to be made even if they were not willed, why then would we speak of **free choice** <note>original: "liberi arbitrij"</note> alongside Divine Providence? If Divine Providence rules, it would seem that nothing could be lost or changed by free choice.

<column-break/>

This is left to the judgment of God, and I wish for no one to seem higher than another. It does not escape anyone that **Divine Providence** is known to God long before a person's birth <note>original: "ortu"</note>. There are markers or "signifiers" in every place regarding fortune, but the counsel of the Master must be learned, because God may will differently than we do concerning our choices <note>original: "electione"</note>.

Through obstinacies and oppositions, the difficulty of **free choice** <note>original: "libris arbitrij"</note> is enclosed here. Does this take away the liberty of the individual? Some argue that humans are saved by judgment, while others are like those on a ship <note>original: "nau'gu't'" (navigantes)</note> who are saved from the waves by a power they did not choose. Some are led to one fate, others to another. 

This brings us to the question of the "hour." We consider the defect or the grace of those who are moved by the "wheel" <note>original: "rotu"</note> of fortune. Does a person choose the hour of their own birth? We see the "hour of the king" or the hour of the commoner. One does not choose the hours poured out for them. **Providence** and the Creator arrange it so that good things are conferred. It is a fraud of the astrologers <note>original: "astiolog[i]"</note> to suggest that one chooses the hour. We must understand that these "signifiers" in the [astrological] figures are placed there by the Creator. Even if one appears a fool or a pauper in his fortune—perhaps under the influence of Mars <note>original: "martib'"</note>—this is directed toward the "blood" <note>The text here becomes very abbreviated, likely discussing the biological or 'sanguine' temperament determined at birth.</note> of the man.

<summary>This page explores the tension between Divine Providence and Free Will, specifically addressing whether the conditions of one's birth (poverty, wealth, or timing) are predestined or chosen. It argues that while astrological "signifiers" exist, they are tools of God's providence rather than forces that negate human liberty or divine judgment.</summary>

## On the Influence of the Moon and Astronomical Images

It should be known that when the **Moon** resides [in a sign], it greatly restricts the operation of purging <note>Refers to medical bloodletting or the administration of laxatives based on the lunar cycle.</note>; likewise in the operation of **surgery** <note>original: "alur-gie," likely a corruption of "cyrurgie"</note>, a person must act cautiously then. One should know in which sign the Moon resides regarding the limbs of the body, because whoever applies iron <note>original: "ducere cum ferro," meaning to perform surgery or use a scalpel.</note> to a limb when the Moon is in its governing sign provokes such great pain, etc. I dare say I have seen infinite damages occur because of this, through open medicine which carries many dangers. For instance, many have threatened their own arms when the Moon was in **Gemini**, or have suffered manifest sickness when they were treated on the arms or elsewhere. They burned their shins and arms <note>Possibly referring to cauterization</note>... it was said that a certain poor man had fistulas for many years because an incision was made while the Moon was in **Scorpio**, which governs the private parts. This was done by a certain physician... who was a master of medicine.

I do not defend the use of **astrological images** <note>original: "ymaginat[ibus] astronomicis," referring to talismans engraved under specific planetary alignments.</note> and their power regarding great works except through what is stated above... for that cause is twofold.

### Here begins the commendation of Astronomy and the fundamentals of the king, etc.

undoubtedly the influence of the spheres is not excluded. In **geomancy** <note>A form of divination that interprets patterns of dots in the sand or earth.</note> I find no such certainty, but I trust in the state [of the heavens] and the day and the hour which they establish, because they say it is a joy that even the smallest reason for things can be provided quickly in time. It is not so with frivolous things, which one should prefer over the true path of truth. Regarding **chiromancy** <note>Palmistry; the study of the hand to determine character or fate.</note>, I shall provide a determination for the present, because it is perhaps proven and physical, as it is seen to be gathered from the signs of the astronomer <note>original: "astronimagister," a master of stars.</note> over the body and the soul. Since characters are generated rather from the shapes of the body which were previously formed by the stars, both are caused by the same principles.

**Here ends the treatise of Albumasar the Great** <note>original: "alb bimagnu," referring to Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), the most influential Persian astrologer in the medieval Latin world.</note> **on the reputations and properties of these things; praise be to God.**

<column-break/>

**In the beginning**
God created the heaven and the earth. It is customary, however, in the most clear manuscripts of sacred writing and books, to make certain prefaces or introductions in the process of the work, etc. And indeed, this is a praiseworthy thing. For just as in speech one must provide a prologue, so too in flute-playing <note>original: "fistulaconibus," referring to the playing of pipes or flutes.</note> one provides a prelude. This is done so that the listener, who may have been long occupied or detained by other matters, may be brought to a state of attention and certainty by the prelude of the prologue, through which they are introduced for the first time to the specific treatise being discussed.

And because every prologue must be adapted to the final purpose, it shall be separated from those things which might conflict with it. Therefore, in this introduction, I have placed the faculty of the **mathematical arts** <note>In the medieval university, the "mathematical faculty" referred to the Quadrivium: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</note>... <unclear>pabi matia fact- tate</unclear>... because it makes one mindful of... <unclear>ato du</unclear>... which leads to the public... and because it invades many ways and wonderful teachers... <unclear>cologiago</unclear>... it leads me to the purpose of the generation of the mathematical faculty, about which many can say different things.

Since in noble things themselves... <unclear>dispe dou genobi</unclear>... by which the external passions which are within the subject are presented. Thus, from the preamble concerning the earth and the subjects in mathematics, its parts are distinguished... <unclear>aporta su actu</unclear>. In this way, the nobility and excellence [of this science] are understood through the nobility of others in the passing of goods, through which our mathematics or astronomy is established from our own...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nobility of the celestial realm and the mathematical arts. It transitions from a philosophical defense of the heavens as God’s creation into a formal definition of the "Quadrivium"—the four mathematical sciences of the Liberal Arts—explaining how arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy are categorized by their relationship to number and motion.</meta>

Not unworthily of his eloquence, all things are subject to his majesty and sovereign power <note>The OCR reads "impio," but in this context of majesty, it likely refers to "imperio" or divine command.</note>. Thus he says that it was in our nature for the voice to remain within the boundaries of heaven. For the heaven was brought forth by God himself, not by its own actions, but for the demonstration of all things, an art which was apparent to God alone. And even though the heaven was then created, reason shows it was not made by chance, as appears to the philosophers, but was intended to be permanent. For as the philosophers wish, each thing is distinct in its members, of which the author is the governor; the corruptible membrane is responded to, as he says by comparison, for I do not wish the philosopher to wander from how it was administered, but rather to look to the presence of the whole work. And how all things flow according to the will of God, so that he speaks of his power. 

**Fourthly**, he resolves from the Lord that those things which are subject to the measure of time are either opportune or hurried in their operation. Our learned men are also accustomed to making a first scattering <note>Likely referring to the dissemination of knowledge or seeds of thought.</note>, so that they might prepare the good of the just, through which they can perform difficult tasks, even through innumerable and subtle scatterings. So, as the glory under the world emitted the heaven, so that by its mediation the influence might be multiplied here in the miracle of the stars, they are produced for glory from various things, varied and innumerable, even infinite. From here proceeds the philosophy of the world, where it is said that Christ himself enjoyed the lower world insofar as the superior world might flow into it, and in the first principles of mathematics he is named as the heir of this world. Thus, therefore, through mathematics itself, which is immovably noble, he rendered a reason concerning the mode of proceeding. This is the pure mathematical theory.

<column-break/>

Through the quantity of the author, he renders the first causes, which have their own limitations through the most powerful demonstrations of time. He who denies these cannot deny the dignity of the faculty of mathematics, which for the present may sufficiently be commended.

**I**t should be noted regarding the aforesaid that the mathematical faculty of which we speak is not <term>astronomy</term> <note>original: "astronomia"; here used to mean the study of the stars and their motions.</note> alone, which he himself established, but it is distinguished into the <term>Liberal Arts</term> <note>The seven subjects of medieval education, divided into the Trivium (language) and the Quadrivium (mathematics).</note>. Of these, the four well-known mathematical branches—arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy—all agree in this: that they all serve to distinguish their own species through rational demonstrations, over which Philosophy is the leader, as is shown elsewhere. 

Reason receives the species of each science according to how the subject is considered. If it is considered absolutely as number, it is <term>arithmetic</term> <note>original: "arithmetica"</note>, which considers number according to its applied properties, such as even and odd, prime and composite, and the like. 

But if number is considered in relation to sound, it is <term>music</term> <note>original: "musica"</note>, which considers relative number in respect to sounds and musical proportions, such as the tone, the <term>semitone</term> <note>original: "hemitonium"; a half-step.</note>, the <term>diatessaron</term> <note>The interval of a fourth.</note>, the <term>diapente</term> <note>The interval of a fifth.</note>, and the <term>diapason</term> <note>The interval of an octave.</note>, etc. 

Similarly, quantity can be perceived in two ways: as immobile or as mobile. If it is immobile (that is, without motion), it belongs to <term>geometry</term> <note>original: "geometria"</note>, which considers terrestrial quantity, the magnitude of bodies, and figures, recognizing the triangle, the square, the rectangle, and distinguishing their species. 

If, however, the quantity is perceived as being in motion, it is <term>astronomy</term>, which investigates the magnitude of the celestial bodies and their movements...

<meta>This page transitions from the philosophical foundations of the Liberal Arts to specific astronomical calculations. ...considers a few spheres throughout the heart of the world and seeks divine reason through the **Liberal Arts** <term>artes liberales: the traditional curriculum of seven subjects, including the mathematical "quadrivium" discussed on the previous page</term>. It is a world that is scarcely understood except through the same God. With the provident ones driven out, all those who are concerned with the quantity of the world agree that goodness exists in motion. When time is considered in the broadest sense, starting from the **first motion** <term>primo motu: the movement of the outermost celestial sphere that drives all others</term> and its measurement, it is nevertheless recently observed that—just as a harpist <note>original: "arpam missor"</note> or one skilled in grammar acts—one must examine and seek out time through the stars. According to their own measure, they must investigate the whole, for it shines according to the grace of the Lord, which clarifies and decorates the whole of creation. Even the followers of **Muhammad** <note>original: "Machometum"</note> look to these same stars, but directed toward a different sphere and using other methods. Let no one dare to call these beginnings false or admire what is wrongly directed, for if one ignores the nature of this birth, they ignore the world itself. Therefore, if anyone deserves to compute our sphere, let them at least learn something of the causes, without which nothing happens in the world. Nor can the properties of the motions be known without this "modern way" of doctrine. For this reason, we shall set forth a "little book of the heart" <note>original: "cordis libellum"</note> regarding the preamble of the world, which I shall carry out well through **calculation** <note>original: "algoring," likely referring to the *Algorismus*, the new mathematical methods using Arabic numerals</note>, as long as God deigns to infuse me with knowledge. To the Lord be grace always.

<column-break/>

**By your instructions**, I have composed this treatise on motions. Because these motions eventually return to their starting points, I have added my own judgments <note>iudiciis: here meaning astronomical calculations or astrological interpretations</note> according to time. These judgments vary across all the inferior spheres according to their motion or according to time, following the opinion of **Thabit** <note>original: "thebiti," referring to Thabit ibn Qurra, a 9th-century astronomer</note> and **Al-Battani** <note>original: "albateny," a famous Arab astronomer</note>. From this, it follows that according to his view, the **fixed stars** <term>stelle fixe: the stars that appear not to move relative to each other, unlike the "wandering" planets</term> do not proceed before 10 degrees and 21 minutes. I say what was once observed; however, some have calculated from the time of the ancient philosophers that the movement was nearly 16 degrees and 17 minutes from **Hipparchus** <note>original: "abrachis"</note> to **Ptolemy** <note>original: "ptholomeu[m]"</note>, just as it was set forth in the second reasoning of the first book of the **Almagest** <term>Almagesti: Ptolemy's definitive 2nd-century work on astronomy</term>. Without this third treatise, from Hipparchus until the later time, the movement was 14 degrees and [certain] minutes.

It is manifest that since the calculation <note>original: "amputacio[n]e," possibly a transcription error for *computatione* or a reference to Thabit's theory of trepidation</note> of Thabit, there is motion; but just as there is motion in the eighth sphere, according to the specific latitude of Thabit, it appears different in the "way of the Arabs" than in our own time. According to the judgments of many years, and to avoid error, **Al-Battani** says that the fixed stars move one degree in 66 years, while **Ptolemy** claims they move one degree in 100 years. Finally, regarding these matters, I was able to experience this in the world through my own consideration. From the observation of Hipparchus until my own observation—which was in the **year of our Lord 1246**—the stars have moved 10 degrees and 12 minutes. 

<margin>Note on the hours</margin>

Through this work for God, I say that astronomers must suppose God's influence. Lately, these are measured according to **mean hours** <term>horis meangles: equal hours of sixty minutes, as opposed to "seasonal" or "unequal" hours that changed with the length of the day</term>. The first hour of the Lord's Day <note>Sunday</note> belongs to the 12th house. Our practice is to calculate the hour of the day of the Moon <note>Monday</note>, and the time of Mercury, and the seven [planets], which were everywhere in these longitudes; but we have proven it just as the ancients did.

For whether concerning the soul's friend <note>likely referring to the "vital spirit" or "breath" (pneuma) often linked to the soul in medieval medicine</note> and its power, just as the soul's light kindles in the blood, so the heart is instructed for these ends. If this should fall upon the body in its great case, and it glows under the stinging rays beneath the Sun, then by this virtue through all animated bodies—and properly those prone to corruption—the time in the world is known, just as the Sun itself is known in **Aries** and in **Pisces**. Those who are born under a better star at that time live more strongly. It is said elsewhere that if one is born under second-rate signs when evil comes, it comes properly. **Planets** always have lordship over all illnesses. **Saturn** <term>Saturn: associated with cold, dryness, and slow, chronic conditions</term> has lordship always over phlegmatic diseases, all sharp and acute aches, and specifically leprosy, hip pain, skin conditions <note>original: "morpheam," a skin disease characterized by discolored patches</note>, and gout <note>original: "podagram"</note>. **Jupiter** has lordship always over the transformation of the blood and everything related to the age of the senses. **Mars** <term>Mars: associated with heat and sudden violence</term> has lordship always over hot fevers and frenzies arising from the blood, and the ending of all things according to the grace of God. **The Sun** has lordship always over hot and dry sicknesses. **Venus** has lordship always over cold and moist sicknesses which happen because of genital issues. **Mercury** has lordship over the passions of the soul <note>original: "passiones aie [animae]"</note>, such as through horrible thoughts and anxieties and all other such things. **The Moon** <term>The Moon: governs fluids and cyclical changes</term> has lordship always over gout and the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note> and always all things that become colder and moister by nature.

This increases or diminishes according to the nature of the humors <term>Humors: the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to control health</term>. When the Sun's rays are removed, the Moon changes all moisture through her own coldness. ### Finding the Beginning through Nature

It seems that when the lord Mars is situated in a house where his part and Libra are in the face <term>face: a five-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign</term>, then one takes through the center of the brain <note>original: "meninges"</note> the melancholic humors <term>humors: the four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were believed to control health</term>, or through that which is without Venus. Under the custody of the Lord, because in that midpoint when he is situated in the House of God—but in Sagittarius and in the face of the Lord—then let it be collected by reason.

Also, under the custody of the rays, let the sage <note>original: "salina"</note> and two pounds be collected through the laws of the midpoint, because the salt is situated in the house of various lords, such as Aquarius or Virgo. When the lady of Mars is in the face, then let the midpoint of the rays be taken from the earth for the sake of receiving. From the medical shop <note>original: "taberna," here meaning an apothecary</note>, it is sublimated <term>sublimated: an alchemical process of heating a substance into vapor and back to solid to purify it</term> through these good things, unless it should be a false thing given to the weight of lepers. Because that which is of the lepers' disease is then brought forth and processed through the coldness of the breath.

Through this, the maturity of those things is sought for the purpose of making a bath <note>original: "balucum"</note> and dispersing the salt. At that time, in that place, it is mixed with whatever was in the vessel and the blood of the little rat <note>original: "sangine ratuli"</note> is added and dispersed in the bath. Then let the whole head be taken from the bath, and they shall be washed with wine and the skin of a goat. You shall keep watch over the evils <note>original: "malos," referring to diseased states</note> and the custody of the same until the berries or weights are delicately removed. It is dedicated to those who work because the earth is under the influence of the unfortunate lords <term>unfortunate lords: malefic planets like Saturn or Mars that were thought to cause hardship</term>. When a malefic is in his own house, he is less harmful than when he is in a foreign house.

<column-break/>

### Concerning the Interpretation of the Moon

Regarding this interpretation, it is said by Zachmael <note>Zachmael or Zael (Sahl ibn Bishr) was a famous 9th-century astrologer whose works were standard in the Middle Ages</note> and is truly related to the Moon in mobile signs <term>mobile signs: Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn, which indicate change and new beginnings</term>, especially in Virgo, because nothing is done in the house of the Moon when the Moon is in Aries. Understand here that it is not true that at all times those things which appear in the middle should be sold at one bright end. If anything is taken at that time at the end of the books, and your Moon was fortunate <term>fortunate: a planet well-positioned to give a positive influence</term>, then if it was of the blood, it is a time of "fantastical" ends <note>likely referring to mental visions or delusions</note>. 

Let nothing be taken unless the end is founded, for then it is not stable. All work, however, must be hurried when in operation. If the Moon is in fixed signs <term>fixed signs: Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius, associated with stability and persistence</term>, then it is like Gemini and lasts for a long time. When the Moon is in these signs, building is difficult. These things cannot be mitigated if they are in the cold or if the action was made through the head and thus the womb is fleeing.

The rest is done when the Moon is in some sign while the Ascendant <term>Ascendant: the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment</term> is fortunate. Otherwise, the work will be hindered. The Moon is hindered when she is combust <term>combust: a planet weakened by being too close to the Sun</term>, or when she is retrograde <term>retrograde: when a planet appears to move backward, often considered a time of confusion or delay</term>. If she is in the head of the malefics <note>the lunar nodes or malefic planets</note>, she receives a direct time. In this way, their will is to flee on the path where the benefics <term>benefics: "lucky" planets like Jupiter or Venus</term> are free.

<margin>Valerius M. <note>original: "Valerius M’", likely referring to Messahalah, an 8th-century Persian-Jewish astrologer whose works were foundational to medieval European astrology.</note></margin>
Messahalah said: At the center of the head, behold the part of the body that was in the world <note>the "macrocosm"</note> and the other part in which the Moon was. And if it was from the house of Aries <term>Aries: the first sign of the zodiac, associated with the head</term>, the Moon was in that joint, and so through the order of the signs.

**Saturn** is a masculine and malevolent planet, having lordship over the fourth limit and ruling over old age. And Messahalah says that it gives a man a melancholic <term>melancholic: governed by "black bile," associated with a somber or introspective temperament</term> nature, tall in stature, narrow, and appearing "burnt" <note>original: "adusta," referring to a dark or weathered complexion caused by planetary heat</term> in his appearance.

**Jupiter** is a masculine planet and has lordship over grace, the blood, and youth. It also rules over beauty, laws, religion, poverty, and the papacy. In its figure, as Messahalah says, it produces a man of a well-composed build, having a white complexion with a reddish tint in the face.

**Mars** is a masculine planet and has lordship over death <note>original: "mrẽ," likely "mortem"</note>, change, anger, and "cholera" <term>cholera: yellow bile, which was thought to cause a hot, aggressive temperament</term>, as well as over wars and battles. In its figure, it produces a ruddy man with red hair and a round face.

**The Sun** is a masculine planet and rules over the spirit, life, light, and splendor. It holds lordship over the heart. In its figure, it produces a man having a color like gold, or dark leaning toward red, with a medium stature and great works.

**Venus** is a feminine planet and rules over many colors. In its figure, it produces a man <note>though Venus is feminine, the text describes the "man" born under it</note> with a white color tending toward dark, with beautiful hair, a round face, and round eyes. It signifies the blood and the masculine planet <note>unclear: possibly a reference to its proximity to the Sun or Mars</note>.

**Mercury** governs subtle works such as the study of philosophy and the arts. In its figure, it produces a man who is sometimes white and sometimes dark, having long fingers. It is a feminine planet <note>Mercury was traditionally considered "common" or adaptable, taking the gender of the planet it was with</note> that can be bent to right or wrong.

**The Moon** produces a white man with some marks on his face... <note>the text here is fragmented</note>

<column-break/>

If [the Moon is] in **Aries**, do not cohabit... <note>original: "noli co..." likely "noli coire," a common warning against sexual intercourse or medical procedures during certain lunar phases</note> because it leads to sharp pain. If in **Taurus**, then the truth of the chest <note>Taurus rules the neck and throat, but often overlaps with the upper chest in some systems</note>. If in **Gemini**, then it is like summer. If in **Leo**, he will rejoice for a long time. If in **Cancer**, do not [act] because you will be noted for death. If in **Libra**, it expands that which is given. If in **Scorpio**, it is moderate. If in **Sagittarius**, it is good for the things one wishes to achieve. If in **Capricorn**, do not [act] because it is evil. If in **Aquarius**, do not doubt because it will be profitable. If in **Pisces**, it leads to various things.

### On the Diagnosis of Dropsy and the Liver

From the colors of the urine proceeding from the patient, one must weigh the corruption of the pure **dropsy** <term>dropsy: "hydrops"; an accumulation of fluid in the body, which medieval doctors believed was caused by a "cold" or "weak" liver failing to process humors into blood</term>. As it has been said, since the natures and the pollutions <note>original: "piazmās" (miasmas)</note>, especially when they occur, cause pain in the lobes of the liver. Because of the debility of the nutritive power, the urine demonstrates a moist color tending toward coldness. 

If the **dropsy** of the body is healthy, it appears thin throughout and reddish, or perhaps sharp and mixed, with an appearance of fever. This is because the place of the **liver** <term>liver: "epar" (hepar)</term> is not localized in its heat. If the dropsy of the body appears febrile with moist urine and a blackness signifying **mortification** <note>original: "mortificacōe"; the death or necrosis of tissue</note>, it is a sign of the mixing of the humors. Because of the weakness of the nutritive power, these humors are retained in the body.

If, however, the dropsy of the body is healthy but the urine is thin and of a leaden color, then the place of the liver is disordered. This indicates a "twisted" febrile dropsy, which is a mixture of cold blood and vapors. It causes **phlegm** <note>original: "flec"</note> to be carried into the sides, and then the urine is of a moderate thickness and reddish color. If the dropsy of the body is healthy and the urine is of a moderate substance and color, it is a middle state. If it were to manifest as a false pleurisy <note>original: "pleu falfum"</note> through that discharge, or if it were merely a false appearance, the color of the urine would be red with a moderate consistency. If the dropsy and the color of the urine are somewhat pale and dewy, or if it tends toward a healthy state in the manner of the body's previous dropsy, then one must consider the humidity of the humors and the dismissal of vomiting...

...of the color of the blood, it will be moderated in the memory of the disease.

# On the Nature of the Planets

The fortune of the day itself <note>This section likely describes Jupiter, traditionally known as the 'Greater Fortune'</note> is **hot and dry** in temperament and holds power in the fourth hour. It harms the right side of the body, yet provides for all and has its dwelling in the world. It governs the sea in <unclear>symis</unclear> and is both **good and masculine**. It is complexioned and stewardly.

### On the Nature of the Planets (continued)

Because of **dryness**, which is a passive quality, his <note>Saturn's</note> will is characterized by the loss of human friendship; he is much quietened by reason while speaking and possesses **deep counsel**. He governs the cultivation of the earth and rare things, possessing a "divine ear" <note>an ability to perceive hidden things</note> and great wealth. He has the power to impress upon the young, though he accepts the healthy as unjust. Regarding fortunes and with "unclean birds" <note>likely a reference to omens or specific animals associated with Saturn</note>, he commits to long-standing customs and states of mind. The suffering of his influences causes **mania**.

The **Wise Man** <note>possibly a reference to Hermes Trismegistus or Solomon</note> speaks much on the anxiety of impending death, like the ruin of heavy weights or stones, or the bite of a serpent. He does not give easily to man, but holds souls in a state of being "sparing and few."

**Hali** <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer</note>, a distinguished man, says that in the opposition of their houses and in his own defense, [Saturn] corrupts and blinds. The **Moon** <note>original: "luna"</note> follows a path of hateful work and natural death, though not a daily death. And if he is **oriental from the Sun** <note>rising before the Sun</note> above the earth, it is good to marvel at his many fortunes and his rising, which receives the perpetual succession of children.

In his own house or in other houses, and then with justice and many [others], he makes fire and various figures; but if he is retrograde, he signifies no light for those walking.

**Almue** <note>term: <term>Almugea</term>; a specific angular relationship between a planet and the Sun/Moon</note> founded the sign... the friendship of the greatest reason... in the 30th way...

<margin>Note that</margin> He says in the 36th book that India is above **Babylon**. **Mars** [governs] the Land of Promise; the **Sun** [governs] the land of reason; **Venus** [governs]... and the **Moon** [governs] the white land of the heart... for the honor of Brindisi... and the land of the <unclear>allopaudans</unclear>. The Moon governs the towns of the Romans... In the west, [the planets govern] **France** and **Spain**.

<meta>This fragment follows the previous page’s definitions of basic planetary interactions like application and radiation. It provides a specialized vocabulary list—likely an index or a glossary—categorizing more complex astrological conditions that occur when planets "touch" or influence one another through movement.</meta>

**Feral** a <note>Latin: *feralis*. In astrology, a "feral" planet is one that makes no aspects (geometric relationships) to other planets; it is considered "wild" or isolated, lacking the support of its peers.</note>
**Connection** b <note>Latin: *copula*. A general term for the bonding or joining of two planetary influences.</note>
**Collection** c <note>Latin: *collatio*. Specifically "collection of light," a technical state where a slower planet receives the light from two faster planets that are not in aspect with each other, acting as a mediator.</note>
**Restoration** d <note>Latin: *redditus*. Also called "restitution of light," occurring when a planet sends its influence back to a planet that has dignity in its current position.</note>
**Prohibition** e <note>Latin: *prohibitio*. An obstruction that occurs when a third planet moves to interfere with an aspect between two other planets before it can be completed.</note>
**Pulsation** f <note>Latin: *pulsatio*. Often called "pushing" (*impulsio*); this refers to the way a planet "pushes" its power or nature onto another planet it is joining.</note>
**Rural Return** g <note>Latin: *redditum rurale*. A rare or specialized term likely referring to a secondary or "common" form of light restoration between planets in specific zodiacal positions.</note>
**Unlocking** h <note>Latin: *reseratio*. The "opening" of a planet's influence or the release of its potential through movement.</note>
**Joining of rural matters** i <note>Latin: *conjunctio rurium*. A technical phrase perhaps indicating the gathering or "collection" of influences from different fields or sectors of the sky.</note>

**Vocabulary:** feral, connection, collection, restoration, prohibition, pulsation, rural return, unlocking, joining of rural matters. <note>original Latin terms: *fferalis, Cupla, Collatio, Redditus, prohibitio, pulsatio, Redditum rurale, Reseratio, Conjunctio rurium*</note>
